additional_notes: Used to correct or contrast: “it’s not X; it’s Y.” It’s the noun + subject marker 가/이 + 아니고 (“is not, and/but”), often followed by another noun phrase or clause (e.g., “…가 아니고 …예요/…이다”). Choose 가 after a vowel-ending noun and 이 after a consonant-ending noun (e.g., 학생이 아니고…).
native_language_example: This isn’t coffee; it’s tea.

meaning: "Whether (you) go or not" / "I don’t care if (you) go or not."
additional_notes: A common pattern is **V-든 말든** meaning “whether someone does it or not; regardless.” With **가다 (to go)** it becomes **가든 말든**. Often used to show indifference or dismissal, and it can sound blunt/rude depending on tone. You’ll also hear it with other verbs, e.g. **오든 말든** (whether you come or not), **하든 말든** (whether you do it or not).
target_language_example: 너 가든 말든 난 갈 거야.
native_language_example: Whether you go or not, I’m going.

additional_notes: Formed from 가다 (to go) + -아/어야 되다 (have to/need to). Used to express obligation or necessity. Often shortened in speech to 가야 돼요 (polite) or 가야 돼 (casual). Can also be used for general necessity (not just a place), e.g., “I have to go (leave now).”
native_language_example: I have to go now.

meaning: 'have to go; need to go' (must go).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity to leave or to go somewhere. Formed from 가다 (to go) + -아/어야 하다 (have to/must). Often shortened in speech to 가야 돼(요). Can also mean you must go (in general), not necessarily right now, depending on context.
native_language_example: I have to go home now.

meaning: 'to bring' (to have/carry something and come with it).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker wants someone to bring an item to the speaker’s location or to the destination being talked about. Often shortened in speech to 갖고 오다. Common patterns: N을/를 가지고 오다 (bring N), 여기/거기/저기(로) 가지고 오다 (bring it here/there), and 주세요/오세요 for polite requests (e.g., 가지고 와 주세요). Composed of 가지다 (to have) + -고 (and) + 오다 (to come), so the literal sense is “have it and come.”
native_language_example: Please bring the book tomorrow.

meaning: 'to have; to possess; to be holding' (state).
additional_notes: From 가지다 (to have/hold) + 있다 (to exist), so it emphasizes an ongoing state: owning something, carrying it with you, or holding it right now. Often shortened in speech to 갖고 있다. Common with objects (돈을 가지고 있다 = have money; 우산을 가지고 있다 = have/are carrying an umbrella).
native_language_example: Do you have some cash on you right now?

meaning: to go to jail; to be sent to prison.
additional_notes: Literally “to go to prison” (감옥 = jail/prison, -에 = to/into, 가다 = to go). Used for being taken to jail or punished with prison time. Often appears as 감옥에 가게 되다 (“end up going to jail”) or 감옥에 보내다 (“send someone to jail”). In everyday speech, 교도소에 가다 is also used for “go to prison,” sounding a bit more formal/official than 감옥.
target_language_example: 그는 사기를 쳐서 결국 감옥에 갔어요.
native_language_example: He committed fraud, so he ended up going to jail.

additional_notes: Casual spoken phrase. 같은 means “same/like,” and 거 is a shortened form of 것 (“thing”). Used to refer vaguely to a type/category (“something like that”), or to say it’s identical/similar to another thing (“the same thing”). Often appears as 같은 거(예요/야) or 같은 거 아니야?
native_language_example: I’ll have the same thing too.

additional_notes: Spoken/conversational form of **같은 것은** (or **같은 거는/같은 건요** depending on particle). **같은** means “like/such,” and **건** is a contraction of **것은** (“thing” + topic). Used to refer to categories or examples: “stuff like that,” “something like that,” often to generalize or downplay. It can be followed by particles (e.g., **같은 건/같은 건요/같은 건 별로…**).
target_language_example: 매운 음식 같은 건 잘 못 먹어요.
native_language_example: I can’t really eat things like spicy food.

additional_notes: 같은 means “same” or “like,” and 걸 is a shortened form of 것을 (“a thing” + object marker). Together, 같은 걸 is commonly used to mean “something like that/this” when the exact thing isn’t specified, often implying “that kind of thing.” It can also refer back to something mentioned before (e.g., “stuff like that”). Often followed by verbs like 하다 (do), 좋아하다 (like), 먹다 (eat), etc.
native_language_example: I often do that kind of thing.

additional_notes: Literally “same thing.” Used to talk about something of the same kind, or to refer vaguely to an example (“things like that”). Often appears with particles: 같은 것만 (“only the same things”), 같은 거(것) (“a similar thing/that kind of thing”; 거 is a casual spoken form of 것), 같은 거예요 (“It’s the same thing.”). Also used after a noun to mean “something like ~”: 영화 같은 것 (“something like a movie”).
target_language_example: 저는 매일 비슷한 일, 같은 것만 해요.
native_language_example: I do similar work, the same thing, every day.

additional_notes: 같은 means “same” or “like,” and 게 is a casual form of 것(thing) + the subject marker 가(=게 in speech). Together, 같은 게 is used to give examples or talk about “stuff like that,” often with a noun before it: 커피 같은 게 (“something like coffee”), 영화 같은 게 (“things like movies”). It’s informal/casual and commonly appears mid-sentence. Often followed by 있다/없다 (“there is/isn’t”), 필요하다 (“need”), or 좋아하다 (“like”).
native_language_example: Do you have something like coffee?

meaning: the same person; a person like that.
additional_notes: Literally “same + person.” Often used with context to mean “that kind of person / someone like that,” especially with 말이야 (“you know”), 또 (“again”), or expressions like 그런/저런 (“such”). It can also mean “the same person” when comparing identity (e.g., in photos, records, or meetings).
target_language_example: 사진 속 사람이랑 지금 앞에 있는 사람이 같은 사람이에요.
native_language_example: The person in the photo and the person in front of us now are the same person.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or state that you and someone else will go to the same place together. Often used as 같이 가요? (“Shall we go together?”) or 같이 가자 (“Let’s go together,” casual). You can specify the person with -랑/하고/와: 친구랑 같이 가요 (“I’ll go with a friend”).
native_language_example: Let’s go together.

meaning: to do (something) together; to do it with someone.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or state doing an activity together. Common patterns: 같이 하자/같이 해요 (“Let’s do it together”), 같이 할래요? (“Do you want to do it together?”), 저랑 같이 해요 (“Do it with me”). Often interchangeable with 함께 하다 (a bit more formal).
native_language_example: Let’s do this project together.

additional_notes: Literally “dog-like” (개 = dog, 같은 = like), but commonly used as a harsh, vulgar insult meaning something is terrible or contemptible. Often appears before a noun: 개 같은 놈/년 (“shitty guy/bitch”), 개 같은 소리 (“bullshit”). Avoid in polite conversation.
native_language_example: Don’t say that bullshit.

additional_notes: Used to say that most of something is included, but not 100%. Often placed before a noun (거의 다 학생들) or used on its own (거의 다 했어요 = I’m almost done). Similar in meaning to 대부분(의), but emphasizes “not completely.”
native_language_example: I’ve done almost all of the homework.

meaning: to lie; to tell a lie.
additional_notes: Literally “to do a lie” (거짓말 = lie, -을/를 하다 = to do). Common in everyday speech. You can also say 거짓말하지 마(요) (“Don’t lie”) and 거짓말이에요 (“It’s a lie”).
native_language_example: Please don’t lie.

additional_notes: A very common verb phrase. It’s often used as 걱정(을) 하다 (the particle 을 is sometimes dropped in speech/writing). You can specify what you’re worried about with -에 대해/대해서 (about) or -을/를 (worry about something). Related forms you’ll also see: 걱정하지 마(세요) = “Don’t worry.”
native_language_example: I worry a lot because of the exam.

additional_notes: Used to soften a statement and show uncertainty (guessing, impression, probability). Commonly attaches to verbs/adjectives with -는 것 같다 (present), -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 (past/looks like), and -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (future/probability). Very common in polite speech as -것 같아요. Also used like "feel like" in contexts such as 집에 가고 싶은 것 같아요 (I feel like I want to go home).
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct an idea: “It’s not that …” or “That’s not true.” Often appears after a clause in the pattern “(… ) 것이 아니다” to say something is NOT the reason/fact. In casual speech it’s commonly shortened to “게 아니다” (e.g., “그게 아니야.”).
native_language_example: It’s not that I’m angry.

additional_notes: Literally “that + who,” but it’s used as an emphatic form of “anyone,” often in negative sentences to mean “no one” (e.g., with 안/못/없다). It can also appear with particles like 도 (“even”) for extra emphasis: 그 누구도 = “not anyone at all / no one.” Common in formal or written style, but also used in speech for emphasis.
target_language_example: 그 누구도 나를 믿어 주지 않았어요.
native_language_example: No one believed me.

additional_notes: Literally 'that where,' but in real usage it usually appears as 그 어디에/그 어디에도. Especially common in the pattern '그 어디에도 ~없다' meaning 'not anywhere / nowhere.' It can sound a bit literary or emphatic compared to just 어디.
native_language_example: There isn’t a person like that anywhere.

meaning: to know that / to know it.
additional_notes: Made of 그거 (“that; it”) + 알다 (“to know”). In real speech you’ll usually hear it as 그거 알아(요)? (“Do you know that?”) or 그거 알지? (“You know that, right?”). The object particle 를 is often omitted (그거(를) 알아). Use 알아요/아세요 for polite speech.
native_language_example: Do you know that?

additional_notes: Used to disagree or correct someone (often: “No, that’s not what I mean” or “That’s not the case”). Common in conversation; can sound blunt depending on tone, so you can soften it with "그건 아닌 것 같아요" (I don't think that's it) or "그건 아닌데요" (Well, that's not it...). Literally "그건" = "as for that" and "아니다" = "to not be".
target_language_example: A: 너 화난 거지? B: 그건 아니야. 그냥 피곤해.
native_language_example: A: You’re mad, right? B: That’s not it. I’m just tired.

additional_notes: Used to correct a misunderstanding or deny what someone just suggested. It can sound a bit blunt depending on tone; often softened in polite speech as “그게 아니에요” or “그런 게 아니에요.” Literally “it is not that,” but commonly means “No, that’s not what I mean.”
target_language_example: 제가 화난 게 아니에요. 그것이 아니에요.
native_language_example: I’m not angry. That’s not it.

additional_notes: Used to correct a misunderstanding or disagree with what someone just said/implied. Very common in conversation. Can sound a bit blunt depending on tone; you can soften it with 아니에요 (No) or add explanation (e.g., 그게 아니라… / Not that, but…). Literal breakdown: 그게 (that) + 아니다 (is not).
target_language_example: A: 너 화난 거야? B: 아니, 그게 아니야. 그냥 피곤해.
native_language_example: A: Are you mad? B: No, that’s not it. I’m just tired.

meaning: “You mustn’t do that / That’s not allowed.”
additional_notes: Used to stop or warn someone not to do something. Literally “if you do that, it won’t do (it’s not okay).” Often said as a firm rule or advice. Common variants: 그러면 안 돼요 (polite), 그러면 안 돼 (casual), 그러면 안 됩니다 (formal).
target_language_example: 여기서는 사진 찍으면 안 돼요. 그러면 안 돼요.
native_language_example: You’re not allowed to take photos here. You mustn’t do that.

additional_notes: A casual way to refer to a type of thing or an example you don’t want to name exactly. Often used when speaking generally, brushing off details, or referring back to what was just mentioned ("that sort of stuff"). Can sound vague; paired with words like 별로/그냥/뭐 to soften or downplay.
target_language_example: 저는 그런 거 별로 안 좋아해요.
native_language_example: I don’t really like that kind of thing.

meaning: “That kind of thing” / “Something like that” (often implying dismissal: “As for that…”).
additional_notes: 그런 건 is a shortened form of 그런 것은/그런 거는 (“as for that kind of thing…”). It’s used to refer to something previously mentioned, and it often sounds like you’re downplaying, rejecting, or brushing it off depending on tone. Common patterns: 그런 건 됐어 (“Forget that / No need for that”), 그런 건 아니야 (“It’s not like that”), 그런 건 나중에 (“That can wait / later”).
target_language_example: 그런 건 됐고, 지금 뭐 할 거야?
native_language_example: Forget that—what are we going to do now?

meaning: "something like that" / "that kind of thing" (as the object of a verb).
additional_notes: 그런 ("such/that kind of") + 걸 = 것을 (shortened form of the object marker) means "that kind of thing" in object position. It’s often used in casual speech, sometimes to dismiss or downplay something: "I don’t do/like that kind of thing." You’ll commonly hear it before verbs like 하다 (do), 좋아하다 (like), or 모르다 (not know).
native_language_example: I don’t do that kind of thing.

additional_notes: 그런 = “such/that kind of” + 것 = “thing.” Used to refer vaguely to something previously mentioned or understood from context. Common in casual speech when you don’t want to be too specific (similar to “stuff like that”). Often appears as 그런 것(은)…, 그런 거(는)… (more casual), or 그런 것들 (“things like that”).
native_language_example: I’m not interested in that kind of thing.

additional_notes: 그런 means “such/like that,” and 게 is a spoken shortening of 것(thing) + particle (often 것이/것을 depending on the sentence). It’s commonly used in conversation to refer vaguely to an example or category: “그런 게 필요해” (I need something like that), “그런 게 아니야” (It’s not like that / It’s not that kind of thing).
native_language_example: I need something like that too.

meaning: “That’s not what it is/means.” “It’s not like that.”
additional_notes: Used to correct a misunderstanding or deny an assumption. Common in conversation when someone interprets your words/actions the wrong way. Often said as 그런 게 아니야 (casual) or 그런 게 아닙니다 (formal). Can also be expanded: 그런 뜻이 아니야 (“That’s not what I meant.”).
native_language_example: Don’t misunderstand. It’s not like that.

additional_notes: 그런 means “such/that kind of,” and 놈 is a very rude word for “guy/fellow” (only for males). Used to insult or show strong contempt, often about someone not present (“그런 놈은 믿지 마.”). Not appropriate in polite conversation; use neutral alternatives like 그런 사람 (“a person like that”).
native_language_example: Never trust a guy like that.

additional_notes: Literally "such words." Used to refer back to a specific kind of comment (often something rude, hurtful, or surprising) that someone said or is about to say. Common patterns include 그런 말 하지 마(요) (Don’t say things like that), 그런 말은 처음 들어(요) (That’s the first time I’ve heard something like that), and 그런 말도 할 줄 알아(요)? (You can even say something like that?).
native_language_example: Don’t say things like that.

meaning: "words like that" / "such a thing" (as something said).
additional_notes: Literally "such words" (그런 = such/like that + 말 = words + -을/를 object marker). Commonly used as the object of verbs like 하다 (to say), 듣다 (to hear), 믿다 (to believe): e.g., 그런 말을 하지 마(요) = Don’t say things like that. On its own, it sounds incomplete and usually needs a verb after it.
native_language_example: Don’t say things like that.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person with certain (usually already mentioned or implied) qualities. 그런 modifies the noun 사람 (“person”), and the tone depends on context—often neutral, but it can sound critical or dismissive (“a person like that”) depending on what was said before. You can also use it when pointing out someone in a situation: “저런 사람” (that person over there) is more explicitly about distance, while “그런 사람” often ties back to a description.
native_language_example: I don’t trust that kind of person.

additional_notes: Uses 그런 (“such/that kind of”) to refer back to a specific type of thought that’s already mentioned or understood from context. Common in phrases like 그런 생각 하지 마(요) (“Don’t think like that”), 그런 생각이 들다 (“to get that idea / have that thought”), and 그런 생각 없어요 (“I don’t have any intention like that”). Often implies disapproval or surprise depending on tone.
native_language_example: Don’t think like that.

additional_notes: Literally “such words/sound.” Used to refer to what someone just said, often to reject it, scold it, or dismiss it as nonsense. Common in patterns like 그런 소리 하지 마(세요) (“Don’t say things like that”), 무슨 그런 소리야? (“What are you talking about?”), and 그런 소리 말고… (“Not that—rather…”). Tone depends on context; can sound blunt when said directly.
native_language_example: Don’t say that. It’s okay.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a type of comment, rumor, suggestion, or story that was mentioned or is understood from context. Common with 하다 (to say/talk), 듣다 (to hear), and 없다 (to not have): 그런 얘기 하지 마요 = “Don’t say things like that.” It can sound dismissive depending on tone.
native_language_example: Don’t say things like that.

additional_notes: 그런 means “such/that kind of,” and 이야기 means “story/talk.” It’s used to refer back to a type of story or topic that was mentioned (or implied) before, often with a distancing or dismissive tone (e.g., “I don’t want to hear that kind of talk”). In conversation, it can also mean “stuff like that.”
native_language_example: I don’t want to hear that kind of talk.

meaning: "that kind of thing" / "something like that" (an event or situation like the one mentioned).
additional_notes: Uses 그런 ("such/that kind of") + 일 ("thing/matter/event"). Common when referring back to a situation just mentioned, often with a negative or surprising nuance (e.g., "something like that happened"). Also used to deny or downplay something: 그런 일 없어요 ("Nothing like that" / "That didn’t happen").
target_language_example: 저는 그런 일 한 적 없어요.
native_language_example: I’ve never done anything like that.

additional_notes: 짓 means “act/deed/behavior.” 그런 means “such/that kind of.” Together, 그런 짓 often refers to a bad or unacceptable action (scolding, criticizing, or warning). Common with verbs like 하다 (to do): 그런 짓 하지 마(요) = “Don’t do that (kind of thing).”
native_language_example: Don’t ever do something like that again.

meaning: “something like that” (a bad thing to do).
additional_notes: From 그런 (“such/that kind of”) + 짓 (“act/deed,” often implying a bad or wrong act) + 을 (object particle). Commonly used when criticizing or scolding someone, often with verbs like 하다 (to do) or 왜 (why): 그런 짓을 하지 마(세요) (“Don’t do that kind of thing”). The 을 marks 짓 as the object, so it typically needs a following verb.
native_language_example: Don’t ever do that again.

meaning: "That will probably be the case" / "It will be so."
additional_notes: Formed from 그렇다 (“to be so/that way”) + -(으)ㄹ 것이다, which often expresses a future prediction or guess (“will probably…”). Used to agree with someone’s assumption or to say something is likely true. In speech, it’s often shortened to 그럴 거예요 (polite) or 그럴 거야 (casual).
target_language_example: 내일 비가 올까요? 네, 그럴 거예요.
native_language_example: Will it rain tomorrow? Yes, it probably will.

meaning: to end up that way; for things to turn out like that.
additional_notes: Used when a situation naturally results in the outcome just mentioned (often unexpectedly or inevitably). Literally “to become like that,” and it commonly appears after explaining reasons or circumstances. Can be used neutrally or with a sense of resignation: “I didn’t plan it, but that’s how it happened.” Often paired with context like 결국/어쩔 수 없이 (“in the end / inevitably”).
native_language_example: Somehow, it ended up that way.

meaning: "not like that" / "don’t (do it) like that" (used before a verb).
additional_notes: 그렇게 means “like that / that way,” and 안 is the common negation meaning “not / don’t.” This chunk is typically followed by a verb (often 하다): 그렇게 안 해요 (“I won’t do it like that / I don’t do it that way”). It can sound like you’re correcting someone’s method or refusing to do something in that manner.
native_language_example: I won’t do it like that. I’ll do it like this.

meaning: to do it that way; to do so.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a previously mentioned method or situation: 그렇게 = “like that / that way,” 하다 = “to do.” Common in agreeing with instructions or describing how something was done. Often appears as 그렇게 하세요 (“Please do it that way”), 그렇게 할게요 (“I’ll do it that way”), or 그렇게 하지 마세요 (“Don’t do it like that”).
native_language_example: Okay. I’ll do it the way you said.

meaning: to not be so; that's not the case.
additional_notes: Used to say something is not true or not correct, often as a correction or disagreement. Common in conversations after someone makes an assumption: “그렇지 않아요” (polite) / “그렇지 않아” (casual). It can also contrast two clauses, similar to “not… but…” (e.g., “A가 그렇지 않다” = “A isn’t like that / isn’t the case”).
target_language_example: 제가 화난 게 아니라, 그렇지 않아요. 그냥 피곤해요.
native_language_example: I’m not angry—that’s not the case. I’m just tired.

meaning: to draw (a picture); to paint (a picture).
additional_notes: Literally “to draw a picture.” 그림 (picture/drawing) + 을 (object marker) + 그리다 (to draw). Commonly used for drawing or painting artwork; you can specify what you’re drawing by replacing 그림 with the object (e.g., 얼굴을 그리다 = draw a face).
native_language_example: I draw pictures in the park on weekends.

additional_notes: A common phrase used to tell someone to stop doing something. 그만 means “stop” and 좀 softens the command like “please” (though the overall tone can still sound annoyed depending on context and intonation). Often used on its own, or followed by a verb: 그만 좀 해(요) (“Please stop it”).
native_language_example: Please stop it. It’s too noisy.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop doing something you find annoying or inappropriate. 그만 means “stop,” and 좀 softens the command a little, but the overall tone can still be firm or irritated depending on context. Often said as 그만 좀 해! (informal) or 그만 좀 하세요. (polite).
target_language_example: 시끄럽게 굴지 말고 그만 좀 해!
native_language_example: Stop being noisy and quit it!

meaning: to stop; to quit; to cut it out.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop doing something, or to say you’re stopping/ending an action. Common as an imperative: 그만해(요) “Stop (it).” It can also mean “quit” (e.g., a job): 일을 그만하다 “to quit work.” Spacing often appears as 그만하다 in writing, but learners will also see 그만 하다.
native_language_example: Please stop now.

meaning: to write (a text); to do writing.
additional_notes: Uses 글 (“a piece of writing/text”) + 쓰다 (“to write”). Common when talking about writing in general (blog posts, essays, articles, messages). You can specify what you’re writing with a noun + 을/를 쓰다 (e.g., 편지를 쓰다 “to write a letter”), and you can mark the topic with 에 대해 글을 쓰다 (“write about …”).
native_language_example: I write texts about travel.

meaning: to write an article (especially a news article).
additional_notes: Most commonly used for writing a news report or press article (기자 = reporter, 기사 = article). You can also say 기사를 작성하다 (more formal). Often followed by where it’s published (신문에, 인터넷에) or the topic (…에 대해).
target_language_example: 그 기자는 어제 사건에 대해 기사를 썼어요.
native_language_example: That reporter wrote an article about the incident yesterday.

meaning: to hold/grab tightly; to get a firm grip (on).
additional_notes: Literal use: physically gripping something tightly (e.g., 손잡이를 꽉 잡다). Common figurative use: to keep tight control or to pull yourself together, as in "정신(을) 꽉 잡다" (“pull yourself together / stay focused”). Often used with objects marked by 을/를.
native_language_example: Hold the handrail tightly so you don’t fall.

additional_notes: Literally “to dream a dream” (꿈 dream + -을 object marker + 꾸다 to dream). Used for dreams during sleep, and can also be used figuratively for hopes/aspirations in contexts like “꿈을 꾸고 있다” (“to be dreaming” / “to have a dream/aspiration”).
native_language_example: I had a strange dream last night.

additional_notes: A repeated form of 나 (“I/me”) used when you want to be chosen, want to do something, or want attention (like raising your hand). Often said in a playful, casual tone among friends or in informal situations.
target_language_example: 청소 누가 할래? 나 나! 내가 할게.
native_language_example: Who wants to clean? Me! Me! I’ll do it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you are doing something alone (without other people). Commonly paired with particles like -만 (“only”) or adverbs like 그냥 (“just”), and often appears with verbs like 가다 (go), 하다 (do), 먹다 (eat). In speech you may also hear the expanded form 나 혼자서 (“all by myself”).
target_language_example: 오늘은 나 혼자 영화 보러 갈 거야.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to go watch a movie by myself.

additional_notes: 놈 is a rough, insulting word for “guy/fellow” and is mainly used about men; it can sound very rude and aggressive. Often used when angry or in casual speech (including joking among close friends), but avoid using it with strangers or in polite situations. Safer alternatives include 나쁜 사람 (“bad person”) or 나쁜 남자 (“bad man”).
native_language_example: That jerk lied again.

additional_notes: Literally 'my + thing'. Used to claim ownership or refer to something that belongs to you. Often said casually as 내 거야 ('It’s mine.'). In writing or more formal contexts you’ll often see it spaced as 내 것, but in speech 내 거 is very common.
native_language_example: That’s mine.

meaning: “How would I know?” / “How am I supposed to know?”
additional_notes: Common spoken reply when you don’t know something and think the other person shouldn’t expect you to. Often said with a slightly annoyed or defensive tone depending on context. More formal alternatives include “제가 어떻게 알아요?” (polite) or “제가 어떻게 알겠어요?” (“How would I know?”). Note: “내가 어떻게 알다” is not natural; in conversation you typically use “알아?” (question) or “알지” (statement: “I know”).
target_language_example:
A: 그 사람이 왜 안 왔어?
B: 내가 어떻게 알아?
native_language_example:
A: Why didn’t that person come?
B: How would I know?

meaning: “It’s so good / I really like it.”
additional_notes: Used to express strong positive feelings about something (taste, experience, situation, etc.). 너무 literally means “too,” but in everyday speech it often means “so/very” for emphasis, not an actual complaint. In casual conversation you may also hear 너무 좋아(요) (“I like it so much / It’s so nice”).
native_language_example: This cafe’s vibe is so nice!

additional_notes: 너희 is the plural/informal “you (guys)” and is used with friends, people younger than you, or in casual situations; it can sound rude to strangers. 둘 means “two” and specifies exactly two people. Often used when directly addressing two people together (e.g., “you two, come here”).
native_language_example: What are you two doing right now?

additional_notes: 너희 is the informal plural "you" used toward people you’re close to, younger, or of lower status (e.g., friends, juniors, kids). 모두 means "all". Together it’s used to speak directly to a group: "you all / all of you". In polite situations, use 여러분 모두 instead.
native_language_example: All of you, be quiet!

additional_notes: 노래(=song) + -(를) object marker + 부르다(=to sing/call). Used to mean “to sing” in general; the object (노래를) is commonly included, though you can also say 노래하다 (“to sing”). In casual speech, it can shorten to 노래 부르다.
native_language_example: I sang songs at a karaoke room with my friends.

meaning: to open one’s eyes; to wake up.
additional_notes: Literally “to open (the) eyes.” Used for physically opening your eyes, and commonly for waking up (often with 아침에/잠에서). It can also be used figuratively to mean “to become aware/realize,” e.g., 세상의 현실에 눈을 뜨다 (“open your eyes to reality”).
native_language_example: As soon as I woke up in the morning, I drank coffee first.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or describe doing something as a group (everyone). Common with suggestions or invitations like “다 같이 가요” (Let’s all go together). Often interchangeable with “모두 같이,” but “다 같이” is very common in everyday speech.
native_language_example: Let’s all take a photo together.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Korean. 다른 = “different/other” and 거 is a casual form of 것 (“thing”), so 다른 거 literally means “a different thing.” Often used when choosing between options or asking to change items. Can appear as 다른 거 있어요? (“Do you have something else?”) or 다른 거로 주세요 (“Please give me a different one / I’ll take another one.”).
native_language_example: Do you have something else besides this?

meaning: 'as for the other thing(s)' / 'the rest (of it)'.
additional_notes: A shortened, casual form of "다른 건(은)" where 건 = 것(thing) + 은(topic). Used to shift topics or contrast one part with another, often implying “everything else besides that.” Commonly followed by statements like "없어" (there isn’t any), "괜찮아" (it’s fine), or a contrasting point: "이건 좋은데 다른 건...".
native_language_example: This is okay, but the rest isn’t great.

meaning: "something else" / "a different one" (short for 다른 것을).
additional_notes: Spoken contraction of "다른 것을" (다른 = different/other + 것 = thing + 을/를 object marker). Used when you want a different option, item, or choice. Often followed by verbs like "주세요" (please give me), "할게요" (I’ll do), "찾아요" (I’m looking for). In more formal writing/speech, you may see/hear "다른 것을" instead.
native_language_example: Not this—please give me something else.

additional_notes: Literally 'different thing' (다른 = different/other, 것 = thing). Used when you want a different option or to refer to something else. Common with verbs like 주세요 ('please give me'): 다른 것 주세요 = 'Please give me another one.' Also used in comparisons: 이거 말고 다른 것 있어요? = 'Do you have something else besides this?'
native_language_example: Do you have something else besides this?

additional_notes: Short for 다른 것이 (다른 것 + 이). Used when contrasting with what was just mentioned, often in requests or questions: 다른 게 있어요? (“Do you have something else?”), 다른 게 필요해요 (“I need something else.”). The 게 form is common in casual spoken Korean; the fuller form 것이 is a bit more formal/written.
native_language_example: Do you have something else besides this?

additional_notes: Literally ‘different place.’ Used to refer to a different location than the current one or than a previously mentioned place. Often appears with particles like -에 (to/at): 다른 곳에 가요 (I’m going somewhere else), or -에서 (in/from): 다른 곳에서 만나요 (Let’s meet somewhere else).
native_language_example: Let’s go somewhere else, not here.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about an alternative option or solution. Often used with verbs like 있다 (there is), 찾다 (to find), or 쓰다 (to use): 다른 방법이 있어요 (There’s another way), 다른 방법을 찾아보자 (Let’s look for another way). Similar to 다른 길 (another route/way) but 방법 is more like “method/approach.”
target_language_example: 이 방법 말고 다른 방법이 있어요?
native_language_example: Is there another way besides this method?

additional_notes: Literally “different person” (다른 = different/other, 사람 = person). Used to refer to someone else (not you/me), often in general statements or comparisons. Can mean a specific “someone else” (another person) or “others” depending on context. Common in phrases like 다른 사람들은… (“other people…”) and 다른 사람 말고… (“not someone else, but…”).
target_language_example: 그 얘기는 다른 사람한테 하지 마.
native_language_example: Don’t tell that to other people.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to ask someone to repeat something or to do something again. Often used politely with 부탁/주세요: “다시 한 번 말씀해 주세요” (Please say it again). Can be shortened in casual speech to “다시 한 번만” (“just one more time/once more, please”).
target_language_example: 죄송한데 다시 한 번 말씀해 주세요.
native_language_example: Sorry, but could you say that one more time?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a repeat or to say you will do something again. Very common in polite requests like 다시 한번 말씀해 주세요 (“Please say it again”). Spacing can vary (다시 한 번 is also common).
native_language_example: Sorry, but please say it one more time.

additional_notes: Literally “to smoke a cigarette/tobacco.” Used for the act/habit of smoking (not for smoke from a fire). Polite: 담배를 피워요. Honorific (about someone you respect): 담배를 피우세요. To ask: 담배 피우세요? (“Do you smoke?”). Common opposite: 담배를 끊다 (“to quit smoking”).
native_language_example: I don’t smoke.

meaning: more; a larger amount / more often.
additional_notes: 더 = “more,” 많이 = “a lot/many.” Together, 더 많이 means “more (than before/than something else).” It’s commonly used with verbs (먹다 eat, 공부하다 study, 하다 do) and in comparisons: A보다 B를 더 많이 해요 (“I do B more than A”). You can also use it as an adverb meaning “to a greater extent” (e.g., 더 많이 필요해요 “I need more”).
native_language_example: You should drink more water.

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to do something sooner or at a higher speed. 더 (“more”) + 빨리 (“quickly/early”), so it can also imply “earlier” depending on context (e.g., “come earlier”). Often used with verbs: 더 빨리 가세요 (go faster), 더 빨리 와 주세요 (please come sooner).
native_language_example: Please speak a little faster.

meaning: "anymore" / "no longer"; also "any further" (in negatives or questions).
additional_notes: Used to say something stops being true from now on (no longer), or to say you won’t continue beyond a point (any further). Very common with negative forms: 더 이상 안/못 + verb (e.g., 더 이상 안 해요 = I won’t do it anymore; 더 이상 못 참겠어요 = I can’t take it anymore). Can also appear in questions: 더 이상 필요 없어요? = Do you not need it anymore?
target_language_example: 저는 더 이상 기다리지 않을 거예요.
native_language_example: I’m not going to wait anymore.

meaning: better; in a better way; even better.
additional_notes: Formed from 더 (“more”) + 좋게 (adverb form of 좋다, “to be good”). Used to compare or express improvement, often with verbs like 만들다 (make), 하다 (do), 되다 (become), or 바꾸다 (change). Common in suggestions and goals: 더 좋게 하다/만들다 (“do/make it better”).
target_language_example: 이걸 더 좋게 만들 수 있어요?
native_language_example: Can you make this better?

additional_notes: 더 = "more" and 크게 = "big" used as an adverb ("bigly" → "largely/loudly"). Often used to ask for an increase in volume or size/amount depending on context. Common in requests like (소리) 더 크게 해 주세요 ("Please make it louder") or 글씨를 더 크게 ("make the text bigger").
native_language_example: Please turn the volume up (make it louder).

additional_notes: Used to say that help is necessary. 도움(help) + -이 (subject marker) + 필요하다(to need). Often used as “도움이 필요해요” (polite) or “도움이 필요합니다” (formal). You can specify what kind of help with “~에/에서 도움이 필요하다” (e.g., “이 문제에 도움이 필요해요” = “I need help with this problem”).
native_language_example: I need help with this homework.

meaning: to pay back money; to repay a debt.
additional_notes: Used when returning borrowed money or paying back a debt/loan. The object is typically 돈(을) (money) or 빚(을) (debt): 빚을 갚다. Common patterns: 돈을 갚아 주다 (pay someone back), 돈을 다 갚다 (pay it all back), 돈을 갚을게요 (I’ll pay you back). Polite request: 돈 좀 갚아 주세요 (Please pay me back some money).
native_language_example: I’ll pay back the money I borrowed next month.

meaning: to earn money; to make money.
additional_notes: A very common verb phrase. 돈(을) is the object marker form of “money,” and 벌다 means “to earn/make (money).” You can specify how (e.g., 일해서 돈을 벌다 “earn money by working”) or where (e.g., 회사에서 돈을 벌다 “earn money at a company”).
native_language_example: I’m earning money in Korea.

meaning: to have a lot of money; to be rich.
additional_notes: Literally “money + (subject particle) + be 많다 (many/a lot).” Used to talk about someone being wealthy or having plenty of money. Often appears as 돈이 많아요 (polite) or 돈이 많아서… (“because I/they have a lot of money…”).
target_language_example: 그 사람은 돈이 많아서 비싼 차를 샀어요.
native_language_example: That person had a lot of money, so they bought an expensive car.

meaning: to have no money; to be broke.
additional_notes: Literally “money + (subject marker) + doesn’t exist.” Used to say you don’t have money (in general or at the moment). Common in casual speech; in more polite situations you can say 돈이 없어요. Often followed by 그래서… (“so…”) to explain what you can’t do or buy.
target_language_example: 오늘은 돈이 없어서 영화 못 봐요.
native_language_example: I don’t have money today, so I can’t watch a movie.

additional_notes: Used to make a request or preference sound softer: “if possible, please…”. Often followed by 부탁/요청, or paired with -아/어 주세요. Also commonly said as 될 수 있으면요 (more polite) or shortened to 될 수 있으면 (at the start of a sentence). Similar to 가능하면, but slightly more like “if it can be done.”
target_language_example: 될 수 있으면 내일까지 보내 주세요.
native_language_example: If possible, please send it by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with counters to say you have/need/want two of something. Often followed by a specific counter: 두 개(=two items), 두 명(two people), 두 잔(two cups). In casual speech, 두 개 can sound like 두 개요/두 개요. Literally ‘two + (counter)’, so it’s compositional.
native_language_example: Please give me two of these.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is done two times. Often appears with verbs (e.g., 두 번 하다 “do it twice”), or as an adverbial phrase meaning “twice” (e.g., 두 번 갔어요 “I went twice”). Also used when ordering/repeating actions: 두 번 주세요 “Give me two (of them) / two times,” depending on context.
native_language_example: Please do this twice.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “the second ___” (e.g., 두 번째 사람 = the second person). In conversation it can also stand alone to mean “the second one.” It’s related to the native Korean number 둘/두 (two) + 번째 (ordinal counter).
native_language_example: Get off at the second station.

additional_notes: Used to say that two people/things are included. Often answers a ‘which one?’ question by choosing both options. Common patterns: “A랑 B 둘 다” (both A and B), “둘 다 좋아해요” (I like both), “둘 다 아니에요” (It’s neither / not both—context-dependent). ‘다’ adds the sense of “all,” so here it means “all of the two.”
native_language_example: I like both coffee and tea.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm that something is correct or perfectly fitting (a plan, time, answer, size, etc.). 딱 adds emphasis meaning “exactly/just right,” and 맞아 comes from 맞다 (“to be correct; to fit”). Common in casual speech; in more polite speech you can say 딱 맞아요.
native_language_example: That’s exactly right.

meaning: for the time to come; to be the right time.
additional_notes: Used when something should happen naturally now (because the right moment has arrived), often with a sense of “when the time is right.” It can be used for seasons, life events, or doing something you’ve waited to do. Common patterns: “~할 때가 됐어요” (It’s time to do ~) and “때가 되면” (when the time comes).
native_language_example: It’s time to leave now.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “another” in the sense of an extra or different one: 또 다른 사람 (another person), 또 다른 방법 (another method). Common in both spoken and written Korean. Often contrasts with the first option/thing mentioned, similar to “yet another” or “a different” depending on context.
target_language_example: 이건 좋은데, 또 다른 방법도 있어요.
native_language_example: This is good, but there’s another method too.

meaning: to like (something); to be pleasing to you.
additional_notes: Literally “to enter (your) heart/mind,” meaning something appeals to you. The subject is the thing you like (e.g., “this bag”), and you mark it with -이/가: “이 가방이 마음에 들어요.” Common polite forms: 마음에 들어요 (present), 마음에 들었어요 (past), 마음에 안 들어요 (don’t like). Often used for choosing/buying things or giving opinions.
native_language_example: I really like these shoes.

meaning: “That makes no sense / That’s ridiculous / Unbelievable.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is impossible, unreasonable, or doesn’t make sense (like “No way” or “That can’t be true”). Often said as an exclamation: “말도 안 돼!” It literally comes from 말 (words/speech) + 도 (even) + 안 되다 (not work/not be possible) → “Even words don’t work,” i.e., it’s not even worth talking about.
native_language_example: That’s true? No way!

meaning: to tell/ask someone not to do something.
additional_notes: Used when reporting someone’s request/order not to do an action. It’s the quoted form of the negative command/request “(verb)-지 말다” + “-라고 하다” (“say/tell”). Structure: [verb stem + 지] + 말라고 하다. Often used with subjects like 엄마가/선생님이 and an object like 나한테. Politeness depends on the final ending: 말라고 했어요 (polite), 말라고 했어 (casual).
native_language_example: My mom told me not to go out late at night.

meaning: to listen to (someone); to follow what someone says.
additional_notes: Used for listening to someone’s words/advice/orders. Often implies obeying or taking someone’s advice, especially with parents/teachers/bosses. Common patterns: "~의 말을 듣다" (listen to/follow ~), "말(을) 잘 듣다" (be obedient / listen well), and "말을 안 듣다" (not listen / disobey).
native_language_example: The kids listen to (follow) the teacher well.

additional_notes: A very common verb meaning “to speak/talk” or “to say.” Literally “to do words/speech,” so it’s often followed by what you say: 예) 뭐라고 말을 했어요? (“What did you say?”). Similar in meaning to 말하다, and can also be used with adverbs like 천천히 말을 하다 (“speak slowly”).
native_language_example: Please speak slowly.

meaning: to make sense; to be reasonable.
additional_notes: Used when something is logical/possible or when an explanation is understandable. Often appears in questions/negatives like "말이 돼요?" (Does that make sense?) and "말이 안 돼" (That doesn’t make sense / No way). "말" literally means “words/speech,” so it’s like “it becomes words,” meaning it can be explained convincingly.
native_language_example: Does that make sense?

meaning: to talk a lot; to be talkative (sometimes: too chatty).
additional_notes: Literally “words are many.” Used to describe someone who speaks a lot; depending on tone/context it can be neutral (just talkative) or mildly negative (talks too much). Often used about a person: "그는 말이 많아요". Can also be used in contrasts like "말이 많고 행동이 적다" (talks a lot but does little).
target_language_example: 우리 동생은 말이 많아서 조용할 때가 거의 없어요.
native_language_example: My younger sibling talks a lot, so there’s hardly any time when they’re quiet.

additional_notes: Used to agree that what someone said is correct or reasonable. Often said as a reaction: “말이 맞네(요)” (“You’re right / That makes sense”). Literally “the words match,” but it’s usually about logic/reasoning rather than matching words.
target_language_example: 네 말이 맞아. 그렇게 하는 게 제일 좋겠다.
native_language_example: You’re right. That would be the best way to do it.

meaning: To not make sense; to be unreasonable/illogical.
additional_notes: Literally “words don’t work.” Used when something is logically impossible, contradictory, unfair, or just doesn’t make sense. Common in spoken Korean: 말이 안 돼요 (polite), 말이 안 돼 (casual).
target_language_example: 그건 말이 안 돼요. 어떻게 하루 만에 끝내요?
native_language_example: That doesn’t make sense. How can you finish it in just one day?

meaning: to be quiet; to not say much (have nothing to say).
additional_notes: Literally “there are no words/speech.” Used to describe someone who isn’t talking (either by personality or in a particular situation). Often implies being unusually quiet or silent when speech is expected. Common variations: “말이 없어요” (polite), “말이 없네” (casual observation).
native_language_example: They’re usually chatty, but today they’re quiet.

additional_notes: A casual imperative meaning “don’t speak” or “don’t tell (me).” It’s used with someone you’re close to; to be more polite, use 말하지 마세요. Often said in the middle of a conversation to stop someone from saying something (e.g., a secret, something upsetting).
native_language_example: Don’t talk about that.

meaning: to tell (someone) for them; to let someone know.
additional_notes: A common pattern where a verb + 주다 means you do the action as a favor/for someone’s benefit. 말해 주다 is often used when giving information, explaining, or passing a message. The person you tell is usually marked with -에게/한테 (말해 줘요/말해 주세요 are very common polite forms).
target_language_example: 선생님, 이 부분을 다시 한 번 말해 주세요.
native_language_example: Teacher, please tell (explain) this part one more time.

meaning: “damn bastard” / “that damn guy” (a very rude insult).
additional_notes: A harsh, insulting way to refer to a man (or someone you’re calling a “jerk”), often said in anger. 망할 is like “damned,” and 놈 is a derogatory word for “guy.” Not appropriate in polite conversation; use with extreme caution.
native_language_example: That damn bastard, he’s lying again.

additional_notes: A very rude, angry insult used toward someone (often younger or acting badly). 망할 is like “damned/cursed,” and 자식 literally means “child/offspring,” but in insults it’s closer to “jerk/bastard.” Avoid using it in polite conversation; you may hear it in fights, dramas, or when someone is furious.
native_language_example: You damn bastard, did you lie again?

meaning: to have a headache; (figuratively) to be stressed/overwhelmed.
additional_notes: Literally “the head hurts.” Use it for physical headache, and also casually for mental strain (like when something is complicated or annoying). Common patterns: "머리가 아파요" (polite), "머리 아파" (casual), and "머리 아프게 하지 마" (“Don’t give me a headache / Don’t make this stressful”).
target_language_example: 요즘 일이 너무 많아서 머리가 아파요.
native_language_example: These days I have so much work that I’m stressed (it’s giving me a headache).

additional_notes: Literally “to wash (one’s) head,” but it’s the standard everyday way to say “wash your hair.” Often used with a frequency/time expression (e.g., every day, twice a week). In speech you can also say 머리 감다. Common pattern: 머리를 감고 (then…) / 머리를 감아야 해요 (I have to…).
native_language_example: I wash my hair every morning.

meaning: a few; several; some (a few kinds/things).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “a few/several” items or “some” types (kinds). Common in phrases like “몇 가지 질문” (a few questions) or “몇 가지 방법” (a few methods). It’s a short form of “몇 가지의 …,” and it’s neutral/polite depending on the sentence ending.
native_language_example: I have a few questions.

meaning: how many (items); a few / some (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with countable things. With a noun: "몇 개" can stand alone ("몇 개 있어요?") or you can use the counter form "몇 + counter" (more common): e.g., "사과 몇 개" (a few apples / how many apples) or "사과 몇 개예요?". Often implies an unspecified small number when not used as a question.
native_language_example: How many apples should we buy?

additional_notes: Uses the question word 몇 (“how many”) with 년 (“year”). In questions it means “how many years?” (e.g., asking duration or age in years). In statements, it can mean an indefinite number like “a few/some years,” depending on context.
target_language_example: 한국에 온 지 몇 년 됐어요?
native_language_example: How many years has it been since you came to Korea?

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the number of people. 몇 = “how many”; 명 is the counter for people (more formal; people are also counted with 사람 in casual speech). Often appears in questions like “몇 명이에요?” and can be followed by particles: 몇 명이/을/은, etc.
native_language_example: How many people are here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the number of people, with -이나 adding emphasis (often expressing surprise, "as many as" / "in total"). Commonly followed by a verb like 왔어요 (came) or 있어요 (there are). Similar to 몇 명이에요? but with extra emphasis.
native_language_example: How many people came to the party (in total)?

meaning: how many times; which number (of a sequence).
additional_notes: Used with counters and questions. With actions, it usually means “how many times” (몇 번 가 봤어요? = How many times have you been?). With numbered things (bus/subway/class), it means “which number” (몇 번 버스예요? = Which bus number is it?). Often followed by a noun like 번(=times/number), 버스( bus), 출구(exit), etc.
native_language_example: How many times have you been here?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens multiple times, often repeatedly. It’s formed from 몇 번 (“how many times”) + -씩 (“each; per”), so it can also imply “per time/at a time” depending on context. Common with verbs like 하다 (to do), 보다 (to see/try), 말하다 (to say), 연락하다 (to contact).
target_language_example: 저는 그 영화를 몇 번씩 봤어요.
native_language_example: I watched that movie several times.

meaning: again and again; repeatedly (as many times as needed).
additional_notes: Often used to emphasize repetition, sometimes with the nuance of “no matter how many times.” Common in statements like “I told you again and again” (몇 번이고 말했어/말했어요). It can also appear with -아/어도 (“even if…”) to stress persistence: 몇 번이고 해도 잘 안 돼요 (“Even if I do it over and over, it doesn’t go well”).
target_language_example: 몇 번이고 설명했는데 아직도 이해가 안 돼요.
native_language_example: I explained it again and again, but I still don’t understand.

meaning: 'how many times' (often: 'how many times on earth/so many times').
additional_notes: Used to ask about the number of times something happened. Often adds emphasis, like frustration or surprise (similar to “how many times do I have to tell you?”). Formed from 몇 번 (“how many times”) + -이나 (emphasis).
native_language_example: How many times have I told you!

additional_notes: Used to ask a person’s age. Often appears as 몇 살이에요? (polite) or 몇 살이야? (casual). In very polite situations you may hear 연세가 어떻게 되세요? (especially for older adults). Koreans may also answer with 살 (native Korean counting) or 세 (Sino-Korean), e.g., 스무 살/20세.
native_language_example: How old are you?

additional_notes: Used to ask the hour/time. Often followed by -예요/-(입)니까 (e.g., 몇 시예요? / 몇 시입니까?). You can also use it in longer questions like 몇 시에 만나요? (“What time do we meet?”).
native_language_example: What time is it now?

additional_notes: 몇 means "how many" (question word) or "some/a few" depending on context. 시간 means "hour(s)." Use it in questions like 몇 시간 걸려요? ("How many hours does it take?") or to say an approximate amount of time like 몇 시간 있었어요 ("I stayed for a few hours"). For exact numbers, use 한 시간 (1 hour), 두 시간 (2 hours), etc.
native_language_example: How many hours does it take from here to Seoul?

additional_notes: Used to ask what time something happens. 몇 시 = “what time,” and -에 marks the time something occurs (at/on). Often followed by a verb like 시작해요 (starts), 만나요 (meet), 와요 (come), or 가요 (go).
native_language_example: What time are we meeting?

additional_notes: Short for "모든 것을". It uses the object marker "을" after "모든 것" (“everything/ all things”), often contracted in speech/writing to "걸". Used when “everything” is what someone does, knows, wants, explains, etc.
native_language_example: He knows everything.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning “everything.” Often used with particles like 이/가 (subject) or 을/를 (object): 모든 것이 괜찮아요 (“Everything is okay”), 모든 것을 다 했어요 (“I did everything”). Can also be used in longer phrases like 모든 것 중에서 (“among everything”).
target_language_example: 지금은 모든 것이 잘 될 거예요.
native_language_example: Everything will be fine now.

additional_notes: 쓰다 is the common verb used for “wearing” things you put on your head (hats, caps). It can mean either “to wear” (state) or “to put on,” depending on context. Casual/polite present: 모자를 써요. More formal: 모자를 씁니다.
native_language_example: I wear a hat when I go outside.

meaning: to be unable to eat; can’t eat.
additional_notes: 못 + verb means “can’t / unable to (do)” (often because of ability, situation, or condition). With 먹다, it commonly means you can’t eat due to being sick, having no appetite, being too busy, or sometimes because you’re not allowed to eat something. In casual speech it can also imply “not eating well / barely eating.”
native_language_example: My stomach hurt, so I couldn’t eat anything.

meaning: to not recognize; to fail to notice/identify.
additional_notes: Used when you don’t recognize a person or thing, or you fail to notice/understand something. Literally 못 (“cannot”) + 알아보다 (“recognize/identify/figure out”). Often used with people: 오랜만에 봐서 못 알아봤어요 (“I didn’t recognize you because it’s been a while”). Can also be used for things like a changed appearance, a voice, or a subtle detail.
target_language_example: 머리를 짧게 잘라서 친구가 저를 못 알아봤어요.
native_language_example: I cut my hair short, so my friend didn’t recognize me.

meaning: to not be able to do; to be bad at (doing).
additional_notes: Often used before a verb to mean “can’t” due to inability or lack of skill (not usually about permission). Commonly written together as 못하다 in everyday writing. Use 못해요/못해 for “I can’t” in polite/informal speech. Can also mean “be bad at”: 수영을 못해요 = “I’m not good at swimming.”
target_language_example: 오늘은 너무 바빠서 숙제를 못 해요.
native_language_example: I’m so busy today that I can’t do my homework.

additional_notes: Literally “to bend/fold the knees.” Used for physically kneeling (e.g., in front of someone, to pick something up) and also figuratively to mean “to submit/surrender” or “to yield” (often in the pattern ~에게/앞에 무릎을 꿇다, “kneel before / give in to”).
target_language_example: 그는 상사 앞에서 무릎을 꿇고 사과했어요.
native_language_example: He knelt in front of his boss and apologized.

meaning: “What do you mean?” / “What are you saying?”
additional_notes: Literally “what words/speech.” Commonly used when you didn’t understand, you’re surprised, or you want clarification. Often appears as: “무슨 말(이야)?” (casual), “무슨 말이에요?” (polite), “무슨 말씀이세요?” (more respectful), or “무슨 말인지 모르겠어요” (“I don’t know what you mean”).
native_language_example: What are you talking about right now?

additional_notes: Literally 'what words'. Used before verbs like 하다/하는 거야/했어/할까 to ask what someone is saying, to quote/introduce speech, or to express disbelief/confusion depending on tone (e.g., 무슨 말을 하는 거야? = 'What are you talking about?'). Often appears as 무슨 말(을) and can be followed by other particles: 무슨 말이야? / 무슨 말을 해? / 무슨 말을 했어?
native_language_example: What are you saying right now?

meaning: “What do you mean?” / “What are you talking about?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification or to express confusion/surprise about what someone just said. It’s casual speech (the polite version is "무슨 말이에요?" or "무슨 말씀이세요?"). Often said with a puzzled tone; can sound a bit confrontational depending on context. Literally it’s “What words is it?” (무슨=what kind of, 말=words/speech, -이야=casual ‘is’).
native_language_example: You’re quitting all of a sudden? What do you mean?

meaning: “what are you thinking?” / “what do you think?” (lit. “what thought”).
additional_notes: Often used as a short question to ask what someone is thinking: 무슨 생각 해? It can also mean “what idea/plan” depending on context (e.g., 무슨 생각이야? = “What are you thinking?”). You’ll also commonly hear it with 하다 (“to do/think”) or 있다 (“to have”): 무슨 생각 하고 있어? (“What are you thinking?”), 무슨 생각 있어? (“Do you have any ideas?”).
native_language_example: What are you thinking about right now?

meaning: 'what (are you) thinking?' / 'what are your thoughts?' (used before a verb like 하다).
additional_notes: Literally 'what thoughts (…)' with 생각 (thought) + object particle 을. It’s usually followed by 하다 (“to do/think”) to ask what someone is thinking: 무슨 생각을 해요? / 무슨 생각을 하고 있어요? It can also introduce what someone is thinking about: 무슨 생각을 하는지 모르겠어요 (“I don’t know what I’m thinking / what I’m thinking about”).
native_language_example: What are you thinking about right now?

meaning: “What are you talking about?” / “What do you mean?”
additional_notes: Literally “what sound/words.” Used to show confusion, disbelief, or disagreement with what someone just said. Often appears as 무슨 소리야? (informal) or 무슨 소리예요? (polite). It can be mild or sound accusatory depending on tone.
native_language_example: You’re quitting all of a sudden? What are you talking about?

meaning: "What are you talking about?" / "What do you mean?"
additional_notes: Literally means “what talk/story.” Used to ask for clarification or show confusion/disbelief about what someone just said. Often said as a short reaction: “무슨 얘기야?” (informal), “무슨 얘기예요?” (polite), or “무슨 얘기 하시는 거예요?” (more polite/longer). Can also be used as a noun phrase: “무슨 얘기인지 모르겠어요” (“I don’t know what you mean”).
native_language_example: What are you talking about right now?

meaning: “What are you talking about?” / “What do you mean?”
additional_notes: Literally “what story/talk.” Commonly used to question what someone just said or to show disbelief/confusion. Often appears as 무슨 이야기야? (casual), 무슨 이야기예요? (polite), or 무슨 이야기인지 모르겠어요 (“I don’t know what you mean”). Tone can sound a bit blunt depending on context, so add 죄송한데 (“Sorry, but…”) or 잘 이해가 안 돼요 (“I don’t really understand”) to soften it.
native_language_example: What are you talking about all of a sudden?

meaning: "what’s wrong?" / "what’s going on?"; also "what kind of work/task?"
additional_notes: Literally “what thing/matter.” Most commonly used to ask what happened or what the problem is, often as a full question: “무슨 일이에요?” (polite) or “무슨 일이야?” (casual). With a noun, it can mean “what kind of”: e.g., “무슨 일이에요?” can also be understood as “What do you do for work?” in the right context, but “무슨 일이 있어요?” clearly means “Is something wrong?/Did something happen?”
native_language_example: What’s wrong? Are you okay?

additional_notes: 무슨 means “what kind of” and is used before a noun to ask for the type/category. 일을 is the object form of 일 (“work/job/task”). Very commonly followed by 하다 (“to do”) as in 무슨 일을 해요?/하세요? to ask what someone does (for work) or what they’re doing.
native_language_example: What do you do for work? / What kind of work do you do?

additional_notes: Literally "what thing/work"; used to ask what the matter is or what happened. Very common in questions like "무슨 일이야?" (casual) and "무슨 일이에요?" (polite). Often followed by 있어요/있어? to mean "Is something wrong?"
native_language_example: What’s going on? Are you okay?

meaning: No matter what happens; whatever happens.
additional_notes: Used to express strong determination that something will be done or true regardless of circumstances. Commonly followed by a promise/decision like -겠다, -할 거야, or a statement of resolve. Literally: “even if there is some kind of 일이 (thing/event).” Similar to “무슨 일이 있어도.”
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I’ll keep my promise.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize determination: you will do something regardless of circumstances. Often placed before a promise/plan, and commonly followed by a future/intent form like -겠어요, -을 거예요, or -할게요. Literally “even if there is some kind of 일이 (thing/event).” Similar to: 어떤 일이 있어도.
target_language_example: 무슨 일이 있어도 약속은 지킬 거예요.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I’ll keep my promise.

meaning: to open a door (lit. “open the door”).
additional_notes: 문(door) + 을(object marker) + 열다(to open). Used for opening doors, gates, windows, etc. In polite requests, you’ll often hear/see 문을 열어 주세요 (“Please open the door”) or 문 좀 열어 주세요 (“Please open the door, please”).
native_language_example: Just a moment—I’ll open the door.

additional_notes: Literally “there is no problem.” Used to reassure someone that something is okay or acceptable, or that you can handle it. Common in casual speech; in more polite situations you can say “문제 없어요.”
native_language_example: Is it no problem if I’m a bit late tomorrow?

meaning: to have a problem; there’s an issue.
additional_notes: Literally “a problem exists.” Used to say something is wrong or difficult (with a device, plan, situation, etc.). In speech you’ll often hear it as 문제가 있어요 (polite) or 문제가 있어 (casual). You can specify the topic with -에/에서: 컴퓨터에 문제가 있어요 (“There’s a problem with the computer”).
native_language_example: There’s a problem with this computer.

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason or cause for something, often when you’re surprised, annoyed, or confused. Common in questions like "뭐 때문에 그래?" (“What’s wrong/Why are you like that?”). Similar to "왜" but a bit more like “because of what/what for.” Can also appear as "무엇 때문에" (more formal).
native_language_example: Why are you mad right now? (Because of what?)

additional_notes: Used to ask the purpose or reason for going somewhere or doing something, often with a slightly skeptical or questioning tone (similar to "What are you going there for?" or "Why bother?"). Usually followed by a verb of going/coming/doing: 뭐 하러 가요? 뭐 하러 왔어요? More casual: 뭐 하러 가?
native_language_example: Why would you buy that? / What would you buy that for?

meaning: "How should I put it?" / "What should I say?" (thinking out loud).
additional_notes: Used when you’re searching for the right words, hesitating, or about to explain something difficult to describe. Often followed by a pause, or by words like 음/그러니까. Can also be said as 뭐라고 할까; 뭐라 할까 is more casual and conversational.
native_language_example: This… how should I put it, it’s kind of ambiguous.

additional_notes: A common spoken fragment used when you’re searching for the right words. Often followed by 하지/할까/하나, as in "뭐라 해야 하지?" (What should I say?) or used before continuing your sentence. Literally comes from 뭐라 ("what" + quoted speech) + 해야 ("should do/say").
target_language_example: 이걸 뭐라 해야 하지? 딱 맞는 표현이 생각이 안 나.
native_language_example: What should I call this? I can’t think of the perfect expression.

meaning: "How should I put it?" / "What should I say?"
additional_notes: Used in conversation when you’re thinking, hesitating, or searching for the right words (often before describing something). It can soften what you’re about to say or signal you’re not sure how to express it. Casual spoken style; you can also hear longer forms like "뭐라고 해야 하지?".
target_language_example: 그 사람은, 뭐라고 할까… 좀 차가운 느낌이 있어.
native_language_example: That person is, how should I put it… kind of cold.

meaning: “What should I say/call it…?” (used when searching for the right words).
additional_notes: Often used mid-sentence when you’re hesitating or trying to find an appropriate expression. Commonly followed by endings like “하지/할까/할지 (모르겠어)” (e.g., 뭐라고 해야 하지? / 뭐라고 해야 할까? / 뭐라고 해야 할지 모르겠어).
target_language_example: 이 기분을 뭐라고 해야 할지 모르겠어.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to call this feeling.

meaning: “Believe it or not” / “Whether you believe it or not.”
additional_notes: Used when you’re telling someone something surprising or hard to believe, and you’re saying it’s up to them to believe you. Often said at the start or end of a sentence. Built from 믿다 (to believe) + -(든 말든) (“whether … or not / regardless of …”).
target_language_example: 믿든 말든, 어제 길에서 연예인을 봤어.
native_language_example: Believe it or not, I saw a celebrity on the street yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to point to the exact person/thing just mentioned or the one you mean (often with emphasis). Common before a noun: "바로 그 사람" (that very person), "바로 그 순간" (that very moment). It can also stand alone like "바로 그거야" (That’s exactly it!).
target_language_example: 제가 찾던 건 바로 그 책이에요.
native_language_example: What I was looking for is that very book.

meaning: to have only; there is nothing but.
additional_notes: Used to express limitation: “only X” / “there’s no choice but to…”. Pattern: N+밖에 없다 (only N). Often followed by a negative verb because 밖에 implies exclusion (e.g., 없다/못하다/안 ~). With verbs: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 = “have no choice but to V” (literally, ‘there’s nothing outside of doing V’).
native_language_example: Right now, I have no choice but to wait.

meaning: to eat (a meal); to have rice/food.
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Literally “to eat rice,” but 밥 often broadly means “a meal/food,” not just rice. Used for any meal in casual speech; in polite speech you’ll often hear 식사하다 (“to have a meal”) or 진지 드세요 (honorific). You can specify the meal: 아침/점심/저녁을 먹다 (eat breakfast/lunch/dinner).
native_language_example: I’m eating (a meal) right now.

meaning: to be punished; to receive a punishment.
additional_notes: Literally “to receive a punishment.” Used when someone gets punished for doing something wrong. Common patterns: “~ 때문에 벌을 받다” (be punished because of ~), “~(으)로 벌을 받다” (be punished with/by ~), and “벌을 받게 되다” (end up getting punished).
native_language_example: I broke the rules, so I got punished.

meaning: to want to see (someone/something); to miss (someone).
additional_notes: Literally “want to see.” Used to express that you miss a person (often said as 보고 싶어(요)). Also used for wanting to watch/see something (a movie, a view, etc.). To specify the person/thing, use -을/를 보고 싶다 (e.g., 너를 보고 싶어).
native_language_example: I really miss you.

meaning: to tell someone to look / to tell someone to check it (out).
additional_notes: Uses the quoted-command form “-(으)라고 하다” with 보다 (“to see/look”). It reports or gives a command indirectly: “보라고 했어요” = “(I) told (them/you) to look.” Often implies “go see it and confirm/check it.” Can also appear as “(누구)에게 보라고 하다” (to tell someone to look).
native_language_example: I told you to look at the photo.

meaning: to rain; for rain to fall.
additional_notes: A common weather expression. Literally means “rain falls/comes down,” but it’s best translated as “it’s raining.” Often used in the present progressive as 비가 내리고 있어요 (“It’s raining”), and in past tense as 비가 내렸어요 (“It rained”). You can add time words like 오늘 (today) or 지금 (now).
native_language_example: It’s raining right now.

meaning: to rain; for it to be raining.
additional_notes: Literally “rain comes.” Common weather expression. Use 비가 와요 (polite present) for “It’s raining,” and 비가 왔어요 for “It rained.” You can also say 비가 오고 있어요 to emphasize “It’s raining (right now).”
native_language_example: It’s raining now.

meaning: to cause trouble; to mess up (often by doing something wrong).
additional_notes: Literally “to hit/make an accident,” but it’s usually used figuratively to mean someone caused a problem, made a big mistake, or did something that created a bad situation. Common in casual speech and often implies blame or frustration. You can also use it jokingly among friends.
target_language_example: 걔 또 사고를 쳐서 팀장님이 엄청 화났어.
native_language_example: He caused trouble again, so the team leader was really angry.

additional_notes: Literally “to fall into love.” Uses the particle -에 (“into/in”) with 빠지다 (“to fall into; to get into”). Commonly used for starting to love someone: 누구와/무엇에 사랑에 빠지다 (“fall in love with someone/something”). Often followed by past tense: 사랑에 빠졌어요 (“I fell in love”).
native_language_example: I fell in love with that person.

additional_notes: A common, neutral way to say “to think.” Often used with a clause marked by -고 (e.g., ~라고 생각하다 / ~고 생각하다) to mean “I think that…”. Also used as “to consider” or “to have a thought/idea” depending on context. In everyday speech, 생각하다 is often used instead of 생각을 하다, but both are correct.
target_language_example: 저는 내일 비가 올 거라고 생각해요.
native_language_example: I think it will rain tomorrow.

meaning: to have no intention (to do something); not be planning to.
additional_notes: Often used with a verb in -(으)ㄹ 생각이 없다 (“I don’t intend to / I’m not going to…”). It can also mean “not interested in (that idea)” depending on context. Slightly firm; soften with polite endings like -어요/-습니다. Literal meaning is “there is no thought,” but it’s used idiomatically for lack of intention.
native_language_example: I don’t plan to move right now.

meaning: to think about it; to consider.
additional_notes: A common, polite way to say you will consider something before deciding. Often used when responding to a suggestion or offer (e.g., “I’ll think about it”). Grammar note: Verb stem + -아/어 보다 means “try doing” or “do and see,” so 생각해 보다 is literally “try thinking,” i.e., “consider.” You’ll also hear the past form 생각해 봤어요 (“I thought about it / I’ve considered it”).
native_language_example: I’ll think about that suggestion.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the 3rd item/person/time in an order or sequence. Comes from 세 (three) + 번째 (ordinal ‘-th’). Often followed by a noun: 세 번째 사람 (the third person), 세 번째 날 (the third day). You can also use it alone when the noun is understood: 세 번째예요 (It’s the third one).
native_language_example: I came third.

additional_notes: Used when you physically put your hand up (e.g., in class, to volunteer, to answer a question). Often appears as 손(을) 들다 / 손 들어요 / 손 들어 주세요. Related: 손을 들다 can also mean “to surrender / give up” depending on context (e.g., 경기에서 손을 들었어요 = I gave up).
native_language_example: If you have a question, please raise your hand.

meaning: to stop being involved; to withdraw from (work/responsibility).
additional_notes: Literally “to take your hand off.” Used when someone stops working on something, steps away from a task, or cuts ties with a project/issue. Common patterns: ~에서 손을 떼다 (withdraw from ~), ~에 손을 떼다 (stop working on ~). Often implies ending involvement rather than taking a short break.
native_language_example: I’m going to step away from this work now.

meaning: to hold hands; to join forces (cooperate).
additional_notes: Literally “to hold (someone’s) hand.” Common for romantic or friendly hand-holding: “(누구)와 손을 잡다.” It can also mean teaming up or cooperating, often with organizations/people: “(누구)와 손을 잡고 ~하다” = “to join hands with (someone) and do ~.”
target_language_example: 그들은 환경 보호를 위해 손을 잡았어요.
native_language_example: They joined forces to protect the environment.

additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to express that someone is able to do something or that something is possible. Common patterns: (verb stem)+-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 (can) and (verb stem)+-(으)ㄹ 수 없다 (cannot). Literally “there is a way/method,” so it’s often taught as a set phrase meaning “can.”
target_language_example: 저는 한국어를 조금 할 수 있어요.
native_language_example: I can speak a little Korean.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as the grammar pattern **-(으)ㄹ 수도 있다** after a verb/adjective stem to express possibility or uncertainty (similar to “might” / “could” / “may”). The negative form is **-(으)ㄹ 수도 없다** (“might not,” “may not be able to”).
native_language_example: It might rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: A common verb phrase using the noun 수영 (swimming) + 하다 (to do). Often used with 장소/시간: 수영을 하러 가다 (go to swim), 수영을 배우다 (learn swimming), 수영을 잘하다 (be good at swimming). In casual speech, 수영하다 is also common (same meaning).
target_language_example: 주말에 친구랑 수영을 하러 갈 거예요.
native_language_example: I’m going to go swimming with a friend on the weekend.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for drinking alcoholic beverages. Often used with friends, in invitations, and when talking about social drinking. You can also specify the type of alcohol: 소주를 마시다 (drink soju), 맥주를 마시다 (drink beer). Note the object particle 을/를: 술을.
native_language_example: I drink alcohol with my friends.

meaning: to breathe; to take a breath.
additional_notes: A very common verb phrase meaning “to breathe.” Often used in everyday contexts (health, exercise, stress) and can be literal or figurative (e.g., “to have some breathing room”). Typical patterns: 숨을 쉬기 힘들다 (it’s hard to breathe), 숨을 쉬어 (breathe!), 숨을 쉬고 있다 (I’m breathing / still alive).
target_language_example: 여기 공기가 나빠서 숨을 쉬기 힘들어요.
native_language_example: The air is bad here, so it’s hard to breathe.

meaning: to spend time; to pass the time.
additional_notes: Used for how you spend time (with someone, doing an activity, or while waiting). Very common with 함께 (together/with), -면서 (while doing), and 어디에서 (where). Slight nuance: 시간을 보내다 focuses on filling/using time (often casually), while 시간을 쓰다 can sound more like using time as a resource. Form: 시간을 보내요/보냈어요/보낼 거예요.
native_language_example: On weekends, I spend time with my friends.

meaning: to not have time; to be short on time.
additional_notes: Literally “time + subject marker (이) + not exist (없다).” Used to say you’re busy or don’t have enough time to do something. Often followed by an action with -아/어(서) to explain the result (e.g., 시간이 없어서 못 가요 = I can’t go because I don’t have time). Polite common form: 시간이 없어요. Past: 시간이 없었어요 (I didn’t have time).
target_language_example: 오늘은 시간이 없어서 숙제를 못 했어요.
native_language_example: I didn’t have time today, so I couldn’t do my homework.

meaning: to pay attention to; to care about; to be concerned about.
additional_notes: Literally “to use nerves/mind.” Common in everyday Korean for showing concern or attention: 신경 써 주세요 (“Please pay attention / please take care of it”) and (저) 신경 쓰지 마세요 (“Don’t worry about me/it”). It can be positive (being attentive) or negative (being bothered/overthinking), often with words like 너무 (“too much”): 너무 신경 쓰지 마 (“Don’t worry about it too much”). Conjugates like a regular 하다-type verb: 신경 써요/썼어요/쓸 거예요.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about what they said.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase. 신문 (newspaper) + 을 (object marker) + 읽다 (to read). You can swap 신문 for other reading materials (e.g., 책을 읽다 = to read a book). In conversation you’ll often hear the conjugated form 읽어요/읽습니다 depending on politeness.
native_language_example: I read the newspaper in the morning.

additional_notes:
A very common, neutral expression in daily conversation. 
- Structure: 실수 (mistake) + 를 (object particle) + 하다 (to do) → “do a mistake.”
- Often used with adverbs like 자주 (often), 또 (again), or 일부러 (on purpose—usually with a negative: 일부러 실수한 게 아니에요 “I didn’t make a mistake on purpose”).
- Past tense: 실수를 했어요/했습니다 “I made a mistake.”
- Polite apology pattern: 실수했어요. 죄송해요. “I made a mistake. I’m sorry.”
native_language_example: I made a mistake. I’m sorry.

meaning: “Oh, seriously…” / “Come on…” (expressing annoyance, disbelief, frustration, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation reacting to a situation or what someone just said. Tone depends on context: it can be playful (“Oh come on!”) or genuinely irritated (“Ugh, seriously?”). Often followed by a complaint or a response, and commonly said with emphasis (아, 진짜!). More casual than saying it in a formal setting.
native_language_example: Oh, seriously—are you late again?

additional_notes: Literally “any thing” (아무 “any” + 것 “thing”). It’s commonly used with questions/conditionals to mean “anything” (e.g., “Do you want anything?”), and with negative verbs (안, 못, -지 않다/못하다) to mean “nothing” (e.g., “I didn’t eat anything” = “I ate nothing”). Often appears as 아무것도 (“anything at all”), especially with negation.
native_language_example: I didn’t eat anything. / I ate nothing.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s no problem or nothing special going on, often to reassure someone who’s worried. Commonly appears as "아무 일 없었어" (Nothing happened) or "아무 일 없어요" (formal/polite).
native_language_example: Are you okay? — Yeah, nothing happened.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to say that nobody is able to do something (못 = “can’t,” “unable to”). It’s an incomplete phrase by itself and is normally followed by an action verb (e.g., 알아요, 이겨요, 따라 해요). You can also hear it as 아무도 못 해요 (“Nobody can do it.”).
native_language_example: No one can solve this problem.

meaning: “no one (does/comes/etc.)” (used to make a negative sentence).
additional_notes: 아무도 means “nobody/no one,” and 안 is a common negation meaning “not.” Together, 아무도 안 + verb means “no one does/comes…” It must be followed by a verb: e.g., 아무도 안 와요 (“No one is coming”). Often interchangeable with 아무도 ~지 않아요 (more formal/explicit): 아무도 오지 않아요.
native_language_example: No one is coming to the party today.

additional_notes: Literally “even one person doesn’t exist.” Used to say that no people are present or involved. Often appears as 아무도 없어요 (polite) / 아무도 없어 (casual). Can also describe that no one does something when followed by a verb: 아무도 안 와요 = “No one is coming.”
native_language_example: There’s nobody at home right now.

additional_notes: Very common way to forbid something or say something is not allowed/possible. Literally means “it doesn’t work” (안 = not, 돼 = work/be okay). Often used as a quick warning: “안 돼!” = “Don’t!” / “Stop!” Can also answer a request: “지금은 안 돼요.” = “Not now.” Add 요 (안 돼요) to be more polite.
native_language_example: You can’t smoke here.

meaning: to not work; to not be allowed; to be impossible; (please) don’t.
additional_notes: A very common phrase with several everyday uses. 1) Something doesn’t function: "컴퓨터가 안 돼요" = "The computer isn’t working." 2) Not allowed / prohibited: "여기서 담배 피우면 안 돼요" = "You can’t smoke here." 3) Something won’t happen / can’t be done: "오늘은 시간이 안 돼요" = "I can’t (make it); I don’t have time today." 4) Telling someone not to do something: "안 돼!" = "No!/Don’t!" Polite endings like -요 are common in conversation: 안 돼요. Often pairs with 되다 (“to work / be possible”) vs 안 되다 (“not work / not possible”).
native_language_example: You can’t take pictures here.

meaning: to know (a fact); to be aware of.
additional_notes: The verb is 알다 (“to know”) + 있다, which shows a continuing state: “to know/remember (and still know)”. Often used for knowledge of facts or awareness rather than knowing a person (for people, use 알다 without necessarily emphasizing the ongoing state, or use verbs like 만나다/알게 되다 depending on context). In speech you’ll often hear the contraction 알고 있어요.
native_language_example: I know that fact (I’m aware of it).

additional_notes: From 알다 (to know) + -고 있다 (to be in the state of…). Used in conversation to say you already know some information. Often said as a response like “Yeah, I know.” In casual speech it can sound blunt; you can soften it with 알아요 (polite) or 알고 있어요 (polite but still fairly direct).
native_language_example: I know that. Don’t worry.

meaning: to handle it yourself; to take care of it on your own.
additional_notes: Used when someone is expected to decide and act without needing instructions or help (“You figure it out / take care of it”). It can sound neutral (giving autonomy) or a bit cold/annoyed depending on tone and context. Often said as an instruction: “알아서 해(요).” Literally “know + do,” meaning you know what to do, so do it.
target_language_example: 그건 네가 알아서 해. 나는 지금 바빠.
native_language_example: Handle that yourself. I’m busy right now.

additional_notes: Literally “which side.” Used to ask between two (or a few) options: 어느 쪽이 좋아요? (“Which do you like?”). It can refer to direction/side (“this way or that way”), a choice (“A or B”), or a person’s position/affiliation (“which side are you on?”). Often followed by particles like -이/가 (subject) or -으로 (direction): 어느 쪽으로 가요? (“Which way are you going?”).
native_language_example: Which way does the bus go?

additional_notes: Formed from 어디 (“where/anywhere”) + 보다 (“than,” used for comparisons). It’s used with a comparative adjective/adverb to mean “more/less … than anywhere else.” Common patterns: 어디보다 + (adjective) (e.g., 어디보다 좋아요). Also used as 어디보다도 for emphasis (“more than anywhere at all”).
native_language_example: I’m more comfortable at home than anywhere else.

additional_notes: 어떤 means “which/what kind of,” and 거 is a casual form of 것 (“thing”). Used to ask someone to choose or to ask what type of thing something is. Often appears as 어떤 거예요? (“Which one is it?”) or 어떤 거 좋아해요? (“Which kind do you like?”). More polite/neutral: 어떤 것.
native_language_example: Which one of these do you like?

additional_notes: 어떤 건 is a shortened, spoken form of 어떤 것은 (어떤 = which/some, 건 = 것은). It’s used when you’re comparing or contrasting different items/people/situations: “Some are…, but others are…”. Often followed by another contrast like 다른 건… (“others…”).
target_language_example: 어떤 건 맛있는데, 어떤 건 너무 매워요.
native_language_example: Some are tasty, but some are too spicy.
