additional_notes: Contraction of "어떤 것을" (어떤 것 + 을/를). Used in casual speech to ask someone to choose or specify something, often when selecting from options. In more polite speech you can say "어떤 것을" or "어떤 걸로" (which one, as the means/option).
native_language_example: Which one should I buy?

additional_notes: Literally 'what kind of thing' (어떤 = 'what kind of' + 것 = 'thing'). Used to refer to an unspecified thing, or to ask/specify the type of thing. Often appears in phrases like 어떤 것인지 ('what it is/which kind of thing it is') or 어떤 걸 좋아해요? ('What kind of thing do you like?').
native_language_example: I’m looking for something.

additional_notes: 어떤 = "which/what kind of" and 게 is a casual spoken form of 것("thing") with the subject marker (것이 → 게). Used to ask someone to choose or specify. Often followed by 좋아? (Which one do you like?) or 원해? (Which one do you want?). Polite equivalent: 어떤 것이/어느 것이.
native_language_example: Which one do you like more?

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know who the person is, don’t want to specify, or you’re speaking generally. 어떤 = “which/what kind of” but before a noun it often means “some/a certain.” In questions, it can mean “what kind of person?” depending on context.
native_language_example: Some person (someone) called me.

additional_notes: 어떤 = “some/what kind of/which” and 일 = “thing; matter; event; work.” Together, 어떤 일 is used when you don’t specify details: “something (is going on)” or “some kind of issue.” In questions, it often means “what happened?” or “what’s the matter?” Common patterns: 어떤 일 있어요? (Is something going on?), 무슨/어떤 일이에요? (What happened?/What’s the matter?), 무슨 일 있어? is more common in casual speech.
target_language_example: 무슨/어떤 일 있어요? 표정이 안 좋아 보여요.
native_language_example: Is something going on? You don’t look well.

meaning: “How can that be?” / “How could you do/say that?” (expressing disbelief or reproach).
additional_notes: A conversational phrase built from 어떻게 (“how”) + 그렇다 (“to be so/like that”). It’s usually used as a reaction when something seems shocking, unbelievable, or unacceptable. In real speech it often appears as 어떻게 그래? or in longer forms like 어떻게 그럴 수 있어? / 어떻게 그럴 수가 있어요? (more common and clearer).
target_language_example: 어떻게 그래? 그런 말 하면 안 되지.
native_language_example: How could you do that? You shouldn’t say something like that.

meaning: “How should I put it…” / “How can I say this…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a rephrasing, a careful explanation, or something slightly awkward/uncertain. Often said with a pause: "어떻게 말하면…" and can be followed by "그러니까" (so), "예를 들면" (for example), or a clarification. Similar to "말하자면" or "그러니까" in function. Literally it’s "if I say it how" (어떻게 + 말하면).
native_language_example: How should I put it… it’s just kind of ambiguous.

meaning: "if you think about it" / "depending on how you look at it."
additional_notes: Used to introduce a different perspective or interpretation. Often followed by a contrasting or surprising point (e.g., "어떻게 생각하면 좋은 기회야" = "If you think about it, it’s a good opportunity"). It’s made from 어떻게 (how) + 생각하다 (to think) + -(으)면 (if/when).
target_language_example: 어떻게 생각하면 이 실수도 좋은 경험이야.
native_language_example: If you think about it, this mistake is also a good experience.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as the question form 어떻게 알아? in casual speech to ask how someone knows something, or to say you don’t know. Polite versions include 어떻게 아세요? (polite) and 어떻게 압니까? (formal). Often followed by a clause: 어떻게 알았어요? “How did you know?”
native_language_example: How do you know that?

meaning: “no matter how (you) do it”; “however (you) do it” (i.e., regardless of the method).
additional_notes: 어떻게("how") + 하다("to do") + -든("no matter whether/whatever"). Used to say the exact way doesn’t matter, or that something will be the same regardless. Often paired with a result clause: “어떻게 하든 + (result).” Similar to “어떻게든” (“somehow / by any means”), but 어떻게 하든 focuses on “no matter how,” not “somehow.”
native_language_example: No matter how you do it, you have to finish by tomorrow.

meaning: "no matter how (you do it)" / "however you do it".
additional_notes: Used to say the method doesn’t matter—only the result. Often followed by a main clause like “~하면 돼요/괜찮아요” (it’s fine if…) or “~해야 해요” (you must…). Built with the question word 어떻게 (how) + verb 하다 (to do) + the choice/indifference ending -(으)든지 (“whether… or…”).
target_language_example: 어떻게 하든지 오늘 안에 끝내야 해요.
native_language_example: No matter how you do it, you have to finish it by today.

meaning: “If/how I do it…” / “How can I…?” (introduces a way or method).
additional_notes: Literally “if (I) do it how,” from 어떻게 (how) + 하다 (to do) + -(으)면 (if/when). Used to ask for a method or solution, often followed by 좋을까요? / 될까요? / 할 수 있어요? It can also lead into a suggestion or condition: “If you do it like this…”.
target_language_example: 어떻게 하면 한국어를 빨리 늘 수 있어요?
native_language_example: How can I improve my Korean quickly?

meaning: “how (did it happen that)…?” / “how did you manage to…?”
additional_notes: Often used to ask about the process, reason, or circumstances that led to something (“How come…?”, “How did you end up…?”). Common in questions like “어떻게 해서 왔어요?” (“How did you come/what brought you here?”). It’s built from 어떻게 (“how”) + 해서 (from 하다, “do,” meaning “by doing/so that”).
native_language_example: How did you end up coming to Korea?

meaning: somehow; by any means (no matter what).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize strong determination to achieve something despite difficulties. Often paired with future intention (e.g., -겠다, -을 거예요) or goals/plans. Nuance can be positive (perseverance) or slightly negative (at any cost), depending on context.
target_language_example: 어떻게 해서든 오늘 안에 끝낼 거예요.
native_language_example: Somehow, I’m going to finish it by today.

additional_notes: Used to express strong determination to achieve something no matter what. Often paired with intention/plan expressions like ~할 거예요, ~해야 돼요, ~하고 싶어요. Slightly stronger and more emphatic than 어떻게든.
target_language_example: 어떻게 해서든지 오늘 안에 끝낼 거예요.
native_language_example: Somehow, I’m going to finish it by today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize strong determination to achieve something despite difficulties. Often followed by a future plan or intention (e.g., -겠다, -을 거예요) or a request/command. Literally breaks down as “however (one) does it, even so,” but it’s best learned as “somehow / at all costs.”
target_language_example: 어떻게 해서라도 오늘 안에 끝낼 거예요.
native_language_example: Somehow, I’m going to finish it by today, no matter what.

meaning: “What should I do?” / “What am I supposed to do?”
additional_notes: Often used when asking for advice or instructions. It’s commonly followed by endings like 해요? / 하죠? / 할까요? (e.g., 어떻게 해야 해요? = What should I do?). Grammatically, 해야 is from 하다 (to do) + -아/어야 하다 (have to / must), so it can imply obligation or “the right thing to do.”
target_language_example: 이거 고장 났는데 어떻게 해야 해요?
native_language_example: This is broken—what should I do?

meaning: to come quickly; (welcome) “come in/come on in.”
additional_notes: Literally 어서 (“quickly/please”) + 오다 (“to come”). In everyday speech it’s often used as a welcoming phrase, commonly said as 어서 오세요 (“Welcome, please come in”) when someone arrives at a home, shop, or restaurant. On its own, 어서 오다 can also mean “to come quickly” depending on context.
native_language_example: Welcome! Please sit here.

additional_notes: Used to ask the starting point in time of something. Often followed by a verb or expression like ~했어요/해요 (did/do), ~알았어요/알아요 (knew/know), or ~였어요/예요 (was/is). Can be a neutral question ("Since when did it start?") or show surprise/complaint depending on tone ("Since when do you do that?").
native_language_example: Since when (From when) have you been studying Korean?

additional_notes: Used to say that a short amount of time passed before the next thing happened. It often follows an event or point in time and introduces what happened soon after. Common in spoken Korean; similar to 얼마 안 가서/얼마 안 있다가. Even though it’s made of words like “how much/not/become,” the overall meaning is idiomatic and translates as “before long.”
target_language_example: 한국에 온 지 얼마 안 돼서 친구를 많이 사귀었어요.
native_language_example: Not long after coming to Korea, I made a lot of friends.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the amount or degree of something, often before a verb or adjective. Commonly appears in questions like 얼마나 많이 먹어요? (how much do you eat?) or 얼마나 많이 필요해요? (how much do you need?). It can also be used in exclamations to emphasize a large degree (e.g., 얼마나 많이 좋아하는지 몰라요 = you don’t know how much I like it).
native_language_example: How much water do you drink in a day?

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mark the topic or area you’re talking about (similar to ~에 대해서 / ~에 관해서, but often feels a bit more formal or written). Common in phrases like "~에 있어서는" (as for..., when it comes to...) and "~에 있어 가장/중요한" (the most important in...).
target_language_example: 한국어 공부에 있어 발음이 정말 중요해요.
native_language_example: When it comes to studying Korean, pronunciation is really important.

meaning: to go on a trip; to travel (go traveling).
additional_notes: 여행(trip/travel) + -(을/를) object marker + 가다(to go). Common everyday phrase. Often used with 어디로(where to) or 언제(when): “어디로 여행을 가요?” You can also say “여행 가다” in casual speech, but “여행을 가다” is the standard form.
native_language_example: I’m going on a trip to Jeju next week.

additional_notes: 영화(를) is the object form of “movie,” and 보다 means “to see/watch.” Often used with 같이 (together) or with time expressions (e.g., 내일, 주말에). In casual speech you may also hear 영화 봐요/영화 봤어요.
native_language_example: I watched a movie with a friend on the weekend.

meaning: to film/make a movie (to shoot a film).
additional_notes: Literally “to 찍다 (take/shoot)” + “영화 (movie).” Used for filming or producing a movie (and sometimes a video). For taking photos, use “사진을 찍다.” In conversation you’ll also hear “영화 찍어요/찍고 있어요” for “I’m filming a movie / I’m in the middle of filming.”
target_language_example: 그 배우는 지금 새 영화를 찍고 있어요.
native_language_example: That actor is filming a new movie right now.

additional_notes: Used when you introduce an example to explain something. Often followed by a noun phrase or a full sentence. Commonly paired with other listing words like "예를 들어" (also 'for example'), or followed by examples separated by commas.
native_language_example: For example, I drink coffee or tea.

additional_notes: A common time expression used to say when something happened or will happen earlier today. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis. Can also be used with particles like "오늘 아침에" (this morning, at/in the morning).
native_language_example: I drank coffee this morning.

additional_notes: Uses the verb stem + -지 말다 to tell someone not to do something. For 오다 (to come), this becomes 오지 말다. Common spoken forms: 오지 마 (casual), 오지 마요 (polite), 오지 마세요 (polite/respectful). You can also add a reason: 위험하니까 오지 마세요 (“Don’t come because it’s dangerous.”).
native_language_example: I’m busy today, so please don’t come.

meaning: to wear clothes; to get dressed.
additional_notes: Literally “to put on clothes.” Use it for wearing clothing in general (옷을 입고 있어요 = “I’m wearing clothes”). For the act of changing/dressing, it can mean “get dressed” (옷을 입고 나가세요 = “Get dressed and go out”). For specific items, Korean often uses other verbs: 신다 (shoes/socks), 쓰다 (hats), 끼다 (rings/gloves).
target_language_example: 밖에 추우니까 따뜻하게 옷을 입고 나가세요.
native_language_example: It’s cold outside, so dress warmly and go out.

additional_notes: Casual spoken phrase used with friends, family, or someone younger. Depending on tone and context, it can show concern (“What’s wrong?”) or sound like a mild scolding/complaint (“Why are you acting like that?”). More polite forms: 왜 그래요? / 왜 그러세요?
native_language_example: What’s wrong? Did something happen?

meaning: Why is that (so)? / Why is it like that?
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind a situation or someone’s behavior. It’s a more formal/neutral phrasing than the casual 왜 그래? (“What’s wrong?/Why are you like that?”). Often appears in written Korean, speeches, news, or reflective questions. Similar forms: 왜 그런지 (why it is so, as a clause), 왜 그런 거야? (more conversational).
native_language_example: Why is that? Is there a reason?

meaning: “why (it is) like that”; “why that happened/why that’s the case.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about the reason for a situation, often when the reason is unknown or being explained. It commonly introduces an indirect question (embedded “why”), so it often appears with verbs like 모르다 (don’t know), 알다 (know), 설명하다 (explain), 말하다 (say). Often followed by particles like -는지/-인지 or endings like -는지 알다/모르다.
native_language_example: I don’t know why that is.

meaning: “What’s wrong with them?” / “Why are they acting like that?”
additional_notes: An informal, spoken reaction to someone’s odd or rude behavior. Refers to a third person (them), not “you.” Often used as a rhetorical question showing surprise/annoyance. Similar forms: 왜 그래? (to you/that person), 왜 이래? (why is it like this/why are you like this).
native_language_example: They’re suddenly getting angry. What’s wrong with them?

additional_notes: Used to complain or express frustration that something happened in the worst or most unlikely choice among many options. Often followed by a noun or situation: 왜 하필 나(야)? (Why me of all people?), 왜 하필 지금(이야)? (Why now of all times?). 하필 adds the nuance of “of all (possible choices), specifically this one.”
native_language_example: Why does it have to rain now of all times?

additional_notes: 요리 means “cooking/cuisine,” and 하다 means “to do,” so together it’s the common everyday verb “to cook.” Often used with what you’re cooking: “김치찌개를 요리해요” (I cook kimchi stew). In casual speech, people also commonly say “요리하다” as one word with the same meaning.
native_language_example: I cook dinner at home.

additional_notes: 우리 (“our”) is often used in Korean when talking about close family members, even when you mean “my” (e.g., 우리 엄마 = my mom). 아빠 is a casual/childlike word for “dad”; in more formal situations you might use 아버지. When talking about someone else’s dad, you’d usually say (상대방) 아버지/아빠 rather than 우리 아빠.
native_language_example: My dad went to work.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has good luck in general or in a specific situation. Very common in daily speech. Often used with a reason or situation: “~해서 운이 좋았어요” (I was lucky because…). You can also say “운이 좋네요!” when something fortunate happens.
target_language_example: 오늘은 날씨도 좋고 자리도 생겨서 운이 좋았어요.
native_language_example: Today the weather was nice and a seat opened up, so I was lucky.

additional_notes: Literally “music + (object particle) + to listen.” 음악 (music) takes the object particle 을/를, so you’ll often hear 음악을. In casual speech it can be shortened to 음악 들어요 (“I listen to music”). You can also replace 음악 with a genre or artist name (e.g., K-pop을 듣다).
native_language_example: I listen to music every day.

additional_notes: Literally “to turn on music.” Used for playing music from a device (phone, speaker, car stereo, etc.), not for performing music on an instrument (use 음악을 연주하다 for that). Common patterns: 음악 좀 틀어 주세요 (“Please play some music”), 음악 틀어도 돼요? (“Is it okay if I play music?”), 음악을 크게/작게 틀다 (“play music loudly/quietly”).
native_language_example: Is it okay if I play some music in the car?

additional_notes: A common spoken reaction meaning something is unacceptable, unfair, or not the right way to do things. It’s short for "이건 (정말) 아니야" and is often said with emphasis. Used in casual conversation; to be more polite, say "이건 아닌 것 같아요" or "이건 좀 아닌데요."
target_language_example: 사람들 앞에서 그렇게 말하는 건 이건 아니다.
native_language_example: Saying that in front of everyone is just not okay.

additional_notes: A casual way to say something is wrong, unacceptable, or not what you expected. Often used to object, complain, or express disappointment. Literally comes from 이건(= this thing/topic) + 아니야(= isn’t/it’s not). Politer versions include 이건 아니에요 or 이건 아닙니다.
native_language_example: This isn’t okay. Try it again.

additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention and direct them to something you’re showing or pointing at. Common in casual speech; can also sound a bit pushy depending on tone. Often followed by what you want to say next (e.g., a complaint, reminder, or suggestion).
target_language_example: 이것 봐, 내가 아까 뭐라고 했어?
native_language_example: Hey, look—what did I tell you earlier?

meaning: “What kind of… is this?” / “What is this (supposed to be)?”
additional_notes: Literally “this + what kind of.” It’s usually followed by a noun (e.g., 소리 “sound/talk,” 일이 “thing/situation”) or used with an ending like -이야/-이에요 to show confusion, disbelief, or annoyance—similar to “What the…?” in English (but without profanity). Common patterns: 이게 무슨 소리야? (“What are you talking about?”), 이게 무슨 일이야? (“What’s going on?”).
native_language_example: What are you talking about?

additional_notes: Literally “this-kind thing.” Used in casual speech to refer to an item, situation, or example that’s like the one you’re pointing to or talking about. Often said while indicating something nearby or in your hand. Can also be used when giving examples: 이런 거 좋아해요 (“I like things like this”).
native_language_example: Where did you buy something like this?

meaning: 'something like this' / 'this kind of thing' (as the object).
additional_notes: Contraction of "이런 것을". "이런" = "like this/this kind of", and "걸" is a casual spoken form of "것을" (thing + object marker -을/를). Often used when pointing to or referring to an example, sometimes with surprise/complaint: "How could you do something like this?". Common in speech; more neutral/polite forms include "이런 것을" or "이런 걸요".
native_language_example: Why did you buy something like this?

additional_notes: Literally “this kind + thing.” Used to refer to something nearby in the conversation or situation (often while pointing or giving an example). Common when speaking generally: 이런 것/저런 것/그런 것 (“things like this/that”). Can sound casual in everyday speech.
native_language_example: I’m not good at this kind of thing.

meaning: “a situation like this” / “this kind of situation.”
additional_notes: Used to refer to the current situation (often one that’s troublesome, surprising, or noteworthy). 이런 modifies a noun and means “like this/this kind of.” Common patterns: 이런 상황에서… (“In a situation like this…”), 이런 상황이 생기다 (“a situation like this happens/arises”).
native_language_example: In a situation like this, you have to stay calm.

meaning: to do it like this; to do it this way.
additional_notes: Used when showing or explaining a method, often with a gesture or demonstration. 이렇게 (“like this/this way”) modifies 하다 (“to do”). Common in instructions: you can also hear 이렇게 해요 (polite) or 이렇게 해 (casual).
native_language_example: If you do it like this, it’s faster.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to tell you their name or stating your name. 이름 (name) + 을 (object marker) + 말하다 (to say). Often used as a request: 이름을 말해 주세요 (“Please tell me your name”). In conversation, saying “제 이름을 말할게요” sounds a bit formal/unnatural; people more commonly use “제 이름은 …예요/입니다” (“My name is …”).
native_language_example: Please say your name here.

meaning: to come here; come over here.
additional_notes: Used to call someone toward the speaker (like “Come here!”). Often said as an instruction/command: “이리 와!” (informal) or “이리 오세요.” (polite). Similar to “여기 오다,” but “이리” feels more like pointing/calling someone over. Can also be used in narrative form as “이리 와서 …” (“come here and then …”).
native_language_example: Come here. Sit here.

meaning: There’s nothing wrong; no problem; no abnormality.
additional_notes: Commonly used to report that everything is normal/OK after checking (health, equipment, security, status). Often appears in formal contexts like inspections, medical results, or incident reports. Variations include “이상 없어요” (polite), “이상 없습니다” (formal), and “이상 없어” (casual). Note: “이상” here means “abnormality/issue,” not “more than/above.”
native_language_example: There were no abnormalities in the test results.

meaning: to work; to do work (a job/task).
additional_notes: A very common, neutral verb phrase. 일을 is the object form of 일 (“work/task”), and 하다 means “to do,” so it’s literally “to do work.” Used for working in general or doing tasks, and can refer to having a job. In casual speech, people also say 일해요/일해 (from 일하다).
native_language_example: I’m working right now.

meaning: to shut your mouth; to keep quiet.
additional_notes: Literally “to close (one’s) mouth.” Used both literally (stop talking) and figuratively (keep a secret / stay silent). Often sounds blunt or scolding, especially in commands like “입 다물어(요)!” (Shut up / Please be quiet). A softer alternative is “조용히 하다” (to be quiet).
target_language_example: 이 얘기는 비밀이니까 입을 다물어 줘.
native_language_example: This is a secret, so please keep quiet about it.

additional_notes: Literally “to spread/open (your) mouth.” Used for physically opening your mouth (e.g., at the dentist, to eat, to yawn). Often appears in commands like "입 벌리세요" (Please open your mouth). In some contexts it can also imply “to speak up / say something,” but the basic meaning is literal.
target_language_example: 치과 의사가 저에게 입을 벌리라고 했어요.
native_language_example: The dentist told me to open my mouth.

meaning: to go well; to work well; to turn out well.
additional_notes: Used to say something is going well or has a good result. With machines/systems it often means “to work properly” (e.g., internet, computer, app). Common patterns: 일이 잘 돼요 (work is going well), 잘 돼 가요 (it’s going well / coming along), 잘 되길 바라요 (I hope it goes well), 잘 됐어요 (it turned out well / good thing). Opposite: 잘 안 되다 (“not go well / not work”).
native_language_example: The interview went well.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is not to blame or that something isn’t a mistake. The subject can be added as a topic: 네 잘못이 아니야 (It’s not your fault). In polite speech you’ll often hear/see 잘못이 아닙니다 or 잘못이 아니에요. It can refer to blame (fault) more often than moral “wrongness,” depending on context.
target_language_example: 네 잘못이 아니야. 너무 자책하지 마.
native_language_example: It’s not your fault. Don’t blame yourself too much.

meaning: to sleep (lit. to sleep a sleep).
additional_notes: A very common, natural way to say “to sleep.” 잠 means “sleep,” and 자다 means “to sleep,” so together it emphasizes the action of sleeping. You can change the tense like 잠을 자요 (present/polite), 잠을 잤어요 (past), 잠을 잘 거예요 (future). Often used with 얼마나 (how long), 잘 (well), or 못 (can’t): 잠을 잘 못 자요 = “I can’t sleep well.”
target_language_example: 어제는 너무 피곤해서 일찍 잠을 잤어요.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was so tired that I went to sleep early.

additional_notes: Literally “that child,” but in real conversation it’s a rude, derogatory way to refer to someone you’re angry at (often a guy, but can be anyone). Stronger and harsher than neutral words like 사람 (“person”). If you want a safer option, use 저 사람 (“that person”).
native_language_example: That bastard lied again.

meaning: "Um, you know…" / "Hey, so…" (used to start a topic or get attention).
additional_notes: A very common conversational filler used before you say what you really want to say (to bring up something awkward, change topics, or get the listener’s attention). Often followed by a pause and then the main point. Informal and spoken. Literally comes from 저기 (“there”) + 있잖아 (“it’s there, you know”), but the natural meaning is closer to “you know…” than “over there.”
native_language_example: Um, you know… are you free tomorrow?

meaning: to go over there; (as a command) “Go away!”
additional_notes: 저리 means “over there/that way.” In everyday speech this is most common as the imperative 저리 가! (“Go away!/Get out of here!”), which can sound blunt or rude depending on tone and relationship. A softer alternative is 저쪽으로 가 주세요 (“Please go over there”).
native_language_example: It’s dangerous, so go away!/Move over there!

additional_notes: Emphatic way to say “all/entirely,” often used to mean “every single one” or “the whole thing.” 전부 means “all/entirety,” and 다 means “all,” so together it’s a stronger “all.” Common in spoken Korean; can be used about objects, people, money, time, etc.
native_language_example: How much is all of this?

meaning: to have none at all; not at all (there isn’t any).
additional_notes: 전혀 means “not at all / completely (not),” and 없다 means “to not exist / to not have.” Together, 전혀 없다 emphasizes total absence (0%). Common with nouns: 시간 전혀 없어요 (I have no time at all), 돈 전혀 없어요 (I have no money at all). In speech, you’ll also hear 전혀 + negative verbs/adjectives (전혀 몰라요 “I don’t know at all,” 전혀 안 해요 “I don’t do it at all”), but 전혀 없다 is specifically about “there is/are none.”
native_language_example: I have no time at all right now.

meaning: to get a phone call; (a call) comes in.
additional_notes: Literally “a phone call comes.” Used to say you receive a call (not that you make one). Often appears in forms like 전화가 왔어요 (I got a call), 전화가 올 거예요 (a call will come / you’ll get a call), or 누구한테서 전화가 왔어요? (Who called you?). For making a call, use 전화하다 or (전화를) 걸다.
native_language_example: I got a call from my mom earlier.

additional_notes: A strong way to refuse or say something is not allowed. Often used as a shortened spoken phrase, especially before/with verbs like 돼요/돼 (“it’s okay/allowed”): 절대 안 돼요 (“Absolutely not / No way”), 절대 안 해요 (“I will never do it”), 절대 안 된다 (“It’s absolutely not allowed”).
native_language_example: That’s absolutely not allowed. / No way.

meaning: to get a grip; to come to one’s senses.
additional_notes: Used when someone regains awareness, calm, or self-control (after being shocked, confused, distracted, drunk, etc.). Also used as advice or a scolding: 정신 차려(요)! Literally “to gather/collect one’s mind/spirit,” so it often translates as “snap out of it” depending on context.
target_language_example: 무슨 일이 있어도 정신을 차리고 해야 해.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, you have to keep it together and do it.

additional_notes: Used to clarify, correct, or rephrase what you just said, often after a pause or when you think you weren’t clear. Literally “my words/topic is…,” and it’s commonly followed by -요 in polite speech (제 말은요…) or by a full explanation (제 말은, 제가 내일 못 간다는 거예요).
target_language_example: 제 말은, 지금 당장 결정할 필요는 없다는 거예요.
native_language_example: What I mean is, you don’t need to decide right now.

additional_notes: Used to beg or strongly urge someone to do (or stop doing) something. Compared to just 제발 (“please”), adding 좀 makes it feel more like “please, come on” and can sound impatient or frustrated depending on tone. Often said alone, or before a request.
native_language_example: Please, be quiet.

meaning: to be quiet; to keep quiet.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to lower their voice or stop making noise. Often appears as commands like "조용히 해요" (polite) or "조용히 해!" (casual/impolite). Can also describe doing something quietly/without drawing attention (e.g., "조용히 하세요" in a library).
native_language_example: We’re in class, so please be quiet.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate an additional amount/degree (time, quantity, intensity). Common in requests and comparisons: “좀 더 주세요” (please give me a bit more), “좀 더 크게/천천히” (a bit louder/slower). Often sounds softer/more polite than just “더” (“more”).
native_language_example: Please give me a bit more water.

meaning: to take a look (for a moment); to look/watch a bit.
additional_notes: 좀 means “a bit” and is also commonly used to soften a request. So 좀 보다 often feels like “please take a look” / “just look for a second,” especially in forms like 좀 봐요 (polite) or 좀 봐 주세요 (more polite: “please look/check it for me”).
native_language_example: Please take a look at this.

meaning: to look good; to seem nice.
additional_notes: Used to comment on how something appears (often based on first impression). Literally “to look/seem good,” and it can be about people, clothes, food, a plan, etc. Common patterns: “N이/가 좋아 보여요” (It/you look good), “좋아 보이네요” (It looks good), “뭐가 좋아 보여요?” (What looks good?), “더 좋아 보여요” (It looks better). When talking about a person, it often implies they look well/healthy or their outfit suits them.
target_language_example: 새 머리 스타일이 정말 좋아 보여요.
native_language_example: Your new hairstyle looks really good.

meaning: to not be good; not good.
additional_notes: Describes a negative condition, situation, result, feeling, etc. It’s the negation of 좋다 (to be good) using -지 않다 (do not). Often used in polite speech as 좋지 않아요 or 좋지 않습니다. Can also mean “not feeling well” depending on context (e.g., 컨디션이 좋지 않다 = “to not feel well”).
target_language_example: 오늘은 몸 상태가 좋지 않아서 일찍 집에 갈게요.
native_language_example: I’m not feeling well today, so I’ll go home early.

meaning: “You bastard!” / “You jerk!” (a very strong insult; literally “a guy to kill”).
additional_notes: A harsh insult used when you’re extremely angry at someone. Often said as a standalone exclamation (죽일 놈!) or with 이/그/저 (이 죽일 놈!) to point at someone. Commonly used in drama-style speech; in real life it can easily start a serious fight. Note: 놈 is derogatory for a man/person (roughly “guy” in a bad way).
native_language_example: You bastard, did you lie again?

meaning: to know how to (do something); to think/assume that (something would happen).
additional_notes: Used after a verb in the form -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다. Meaning 1: ability/skill ("can do"), e.g. 할 줄 알아요. Meaning 2: expectation/assumption, often in past tense ("I thought..."), e.g. 올 줄 알았어요 (I thought you would come). The opposite is -(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다 (not know how to / not realize).
native_language_example: I know how to swim.

additional_notes: Stronger than just 지금 (“now”)—it adds urgency, like “right this second.” Common in commands/requests (지금 당장 와! “Come right now!”) and in giving instructions. In more polite speech, you can use 지금 당장 ~하세요/해주세요. Can also be used with 해야 해/해야 돼 to mean “have to do it right away.”
native_language_example: Please come right now.

additional_notes: Used with the particle 을/를 on 지하철 (subway) + 타다 (to ride/take). Very common for public transportation (버스를 타다 = take the bus, 택시를 타다 = take a taxi). Often followed by 어디까지/어디에서/어디로 to say how far/from where/to where.
target_language_example: 저는 매일 아침 지하철을 타고 회사에 가요.
native_language_example: I take the subway every morning and go to work.

additional_notes: A common, neutral verb phrase used in class, meetings, or everyday conversations. The object is 질문(을) (“a question”), and 하다 means “to do,” so it literally means “to do a question,” but the natural meaning is “to ask a question.” You can also say 질문하다 (same meaning, slightly more concise). Polite forms: 질문(을) 해요 / 질문(을) 합니다.
native_language_example: Can I ask a question after class?

additional_notes: 집 = “home/house,” -에 marks the destination (“to”), and 가다 means “to go.” Common everyday phrase; you can also say 집에 가요 (polite). Often used when leaving: 이제 집에 갈게요 (“I’m going home now / I’ll head home now.”).
native_language_example: I’m going home now.

meaning: to go back home; to return home.
additional_notes: Used to say you return to your home (after work, school, traveling, etc.). 집에 means “to home/at home,” and 돌아가다 means “to go back/return.” Common variants: 집에 돌아가요 (polite present/future: “I’m going back home”), 집에 돌아갔어요 (“I went back home”). Similar everyday phrase: 집에 가다 (“to go home”), which is more general; 돌아가다 emphasizes returning.
native_language_example: After work, I’m going to go back home.

meaning: to get annoyed; to feel irritated.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re feeling irritated or fed up (often because of a situation). Very common in daily speech. With a person, it can sound accusatory (e.g., 너 때문에 짜증 나 = “You’re annoying me”), so use carefully. You can also intensify it with expressions like 진짜/너무/완전.
target_language_example: 요즘 일이 너무 많아서 짜증이 나요.
native_language_example: These days I have too much work, so I’m getting irritated.

meaning: to stop/park a car; to pull over.
additional_notes: Literally “to stand a car.” Used when you bring a car to a stop (often to the side of the road) or park it. Common patterns: “(길가에) 차를 세우다” (pull over/stop by the road), “여기에 차를 세우세요” (park/stop the car here). Different from “차가 서다” (the car stops) which focuses on the car stopping by itself.
native_language_example: Is it okay if I stop/park the car here for a moment?

additional_notes: 찾다 means "to look for" or "to find" depending on context; 찾고 있다 emphasizes an action in progress ("am/are/is looking for"). Commonly used when you haven’t found it yet. You can add an object with 를/을: "열쇠를 찾고 있어요" (I’m looking for my keys). Polite present: 찾고 있어요; plain: 찾고 있어; formal: 찾고 있습니다.
native_language_example: I’m looking for my wallet right now.

additional_notes: A common verb phrase: 책 (book) + 을 (object particle, used after a consonant) + 읽다 (to read). Often used as 책을 읽어요 (polite present) / 책을 읽었어요 (polite past) / 책을 읽을 거예요 (polite future). You can swap 책 with other objects (e.g., 신문을 읽다 = to read the newspaper).
native_language_example: I read a book every night.

meaning: from the beginning; from the start.
additional_notes: Used to say something starts at the very beginning, or to emphasize doing something again starting at the start. Often used with 다시 (again): 처음부터 다시 (from the beginning again). Can also mean “from the start (of something)” in context.
native_language_example: Please explain it again from the beginning.

meaning: to do your best; to give it your all.
additional_notes: A common, polite phrase meaning you will put in maximum effort. Often used in promises or encouragement. Typical patterns: “최선을 다할게요” (I’ll do my best) and “최선을 다하세요/다해요” (Please do your best / Do your best).
native_language_example: I’ll do my best for this presentation.

additional_notes: A common, natural verb phrase meaning “to dance.” Uses the object marker -을/를: 춤(을) + 추다. In casual speech the object particle 을 is often dropped: 춤 추다. Tense and politeness change on 추다 (e.g., 춤을 춰요/췄어요).
native_language_example: I danced to the music with my friends.

additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to express desire: V-고 싶다. For example, 가고 싶다 (want to go), 먹고 싶다 (want to eat). You can make it polite with -고 싶어요, and past with -고 싶었어요 (wanted to). The object/thing you want is often marked with 을/를: 한국어를 배우고 싶어요 (I want to learn Korean).
native_language_example: I want to eat Korean food.

additional_notes: Formed from a verb stem + -고 있다 to show an action in progress (present continuous). Often translates as “be -ing.” It can also describe a continuing state/result with some verbs (e.g., 앉고 있다 “is sitting,” 살고 있다 “lives/is living”). In speech, it’s commonly shortened to -고 있어요 (polite) or -고 있어 (casual).
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

meaning: "whether (someone) does it or not"; "do it or don’t" (I don’t care).
additional_notes: Built from the pattern -(으)든 (…or…) repeated: 하든(=whether you do it) 말든(=or not). Used to show indifference or to say it’s up to the other person, often with an annoyed or dismissive tone. Commonly followed by a separate clause like 상관없어(요) (I don’t care) or 마음대로 해(요) (do as you like).
native_language_example: Go or don’t—it's up to you.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to do an action. It’s 하다 (“to do”) + 말다 (“to not do/stop”), so it attaches to the verb stem: 하다 → 하지 말다. In polite speech you’ll often hear 하지 마요 (“Please don’t do it”) or 하지 마세요 (more polite). For a strong command (casual), use 하지 마.
native_language_example: Please don’t lie.

additional_notes: Used to negate actions expressed with 하다 (“to do”), as in 공부하다 → 공부하지 않다 (“to not study”). Often contracts in speech to 안 하다 (more casual) or written as 하지 않아요/하지 않습니다 depending on politeness level. Can also be used with 못 하다 when the meaning is “can’t” rather than “don’t.”
native_language_example: I’m not exercising today.

meaning: 'one thing' / 'one kind'; also used like 'for one thing' (one point).
additional_notes: Literally 한 (one) + 가지 (kind/branch). Commonly used to introduce a single item, reason, or point: 한 가지 질문이 있어요 (I have one question), 한 가지 부탁이 있어요 (I have one request). You can use it with counters or nouns, and it often sets up a contrast when followed by another point (e.g., 한 가지는 …, 또 한 가지는 …).
native_language_example: I have one request.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to repeat something (speech, an action, a song, a photo, etc.). Often paired with a request like 해 주세요 (“please do it”) or 말해 주세요 (“please say it”). You can also use it alone as a quick prompt. Literally “one time more.”
target_language_example: 죄송한데 한 번 더 말씀해 주실 수 있어요?
native_language_example: Sorry, could you say that one more time?

meaning: "I have something to say" / "I need to tell you something."
additional_notes: Literally "(I) have words to say." Used to introduce something you want to say, often something important or serious. Commonly used as "할 말 있어" (casual) or "할 말 있습니다" (formal). Often followed by "잠깐" (for a moment): "할 말 있는데 잠깐 시간 있어?"
target_language_example: 나 할 말 있어. 지금 잠깐 괜찮아?
native_language_example: I have something to tell you. Is now okay for a moment?

meaning: “I have something to say.” / “I need to tell you something.”
additional_notes: Literally “there are words to say” (할 = to do, 말 = words/speech, -이 있다 = there is/are). Commonly used to introduce a topic you want to bring up, often something important or serious. You can add a listener: “할 말이 있어요, 잠깐 얘기할 수 있어요?” (“I have something to say—can we talk for a moment?”). Politeness changes: casual 할 말이 있어; polite 할 말이 있어요; formal 할 말이 있습니다.
target_language_example: 저 할 말이 있어요. 잠깐 얘기할 수 있어요?
native_language_example: I have something to say. Can we talk for a moment?

meaning: to be able to (do something); can.
additional_notes: Made from 하다 (to do) + -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 (to have the ability/possibility). Used to express ability, possibility, or permission depending on context. Commonly paired with an action verb: V-(으)ㄹ 수 있다 (e.g., 가다 → 갈 수 있다). The opposite is 할 수 없다 (“can’t / not able to”).
target_language_example: 저는 한국어를 조금 할 수 있어요.
native_language_example: I can speak a little Korean.

additional_notes: Formed from 할 수 있다 (“to be able to do”) + -면 (“if”). Used to express a condition or a polite preference/suggestion: “if you can/if it’s possible.” Often followed by 부탁/제안/요청, and can appear as “(제가) 할 수 있다면 …” (“If I can, I will …”).
target_language_example: 시간이 된다면, 내일까지 보내 주실 수 있을까요?
native_language_example: If you have time, could you send it by tomorrow?

additional_notes: From 하다 (“to do”) + 보다 (“to see/try”), used after a verb stem to mean “try doing it” or “give it a go.” Common forms: 해 봐요 (polite), 해 봐 (casual), 해 보세요 (please try), 해 보고 싶어요 (I want to try). Written spacing can vary, but in practice you’ll often see it attached to the verb: V-아/어 보다 (e.g., 먹어 보다, 가 보다).
native_language_example: Try this once.

meaning: to do (something) for someone (as a favor).
additional_notes: Used after an action verb stem to mean you do that action for someone else: V-아/어 주다 (e.g., 도와 주다, 알려 주다). It often implies kindness/helpfulness. In casual speech it’s commonly written/spoken as 해주다 (no space). Polite forms are 해 주세요/해 줘요 (“please do it for me”), and past is 해 줬어요/해 줬다.
native_language_example: Please take a picture for me.

meaning: to have to; must (need to do).
additional_notes: Expresses obligation/necessity. Literally “have to do,” from 하다 (to do) + -아/어야 (must) + 되다 (to become/it works out) → “it has to be that you do it.” Common in conversation; often shortened to 해야 돼. Negative is 안 해도 돼/안 해야 돼 depending on meaning (“don’t have to” vs “must not”).
target_language_example: 오늘은 일찍 가야 해서 숙제를 해야 돼요.
native_language_example: I have to do my homework because I need to leave early today.

meaning: to have to; must (be required to do).
additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity. Formed from the verb 하다 (“to do”) with the requirement pattern -아/어야 하다 (“must do”). Conjugates like a regular verb: 해요 (polite), 해야 해요 (polite), 해야 합니다 (formal). Often used with another verb in -아/어야 하다 form: 가야 하다 (have to go), 먹어야 하다 (have to eat). In casual speech, it’s commonly shortened to 해야 돼(요) (“have to”).
target_language_example: 오늘은 일찍 자야 해요. 내일 일찍 일어나야 하거든요.
native_language_example: I have to go to bed early today because I have to wake up early tomorrow.

meaning: to get angry; to be mad.
additional_notes: Very common way to say you’re angry. Literally “anger comes out/arises” (화=anger + -가 subject marker + 나다=to come out/arise). Often used with a cause using -때문에 (“because of”) or with a person using -한테/에게 (“at/with someone”). Also used in negatives and past tense: 화가 안 나요 (“I’m not angry”), 화가 났어요 (“I got angry / I was mad”).
native_language_example: I got angry because of what you said.

meaning: to be effective; to work (have an effect).
additional_notes: Used when something produces the desired result. Very common with medicines, treatments, methods, advice, and products. Often appears as 효과가 있어요 (polite) or 효과가 없어요 (“it doesn’t work”). You can specify what it works for with -에/에게: 이 약은 감기에 효과가 있어요 (“This medicine works for colds”).
native_language_example: This medicine is effective for colds.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a comparison (often with comparatives like 더/덜, -보다, or adjectives like 크다/좋다). 훨씬 means “by far / a lot,” and adding 더 makes the emphasis even stronger. Common in sentences like A보다 훨씬 더 ~해요 (“It’s much more ~ than A”).
target_language_example: 이 카페가 저 카페보다 훨씬 더 조용해요.
native_language_example: This cafe is much quieter than that cafe.
